activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: Gottfried Leibniz introduced the integral sign in 1675, basing it on an elongated letter s because he thought of an integral as an infinite sum.
story:
Ryder had requisitioned the school's only copy of the old calculus text because the new editions were back-ordered until October, and Ms. Nowak had made it clear that the quiz on areas under curves would not wait for shipping. The book arrived with a cracked spine and a previous student's name inked inside the cover, and it sat now on the kitchen table between his elbow and a mug of cooling tea, open to a page of curves that rose and fell like grassland, the graph paper a thin white steppe stretching to each margin.

Chelsey had come over because she understood the rectangles and he understood the limits, and together, in theory, they understood the whole thing. In practice she kept nudging the paper toward him and saying the parts she thought he already knew, which he did not.

"Smaller and smaller slices," she said. "You add them up. That's the area."

"Add up infinitely many things," Ryder said. "That's not adding, that's a trick."

"It's not a trick, it's a limit."

"It's a trick with good manners."

She laughed, then flattened the page with her palm and pointed at the tall thin symbol in front of the dx, the one that looked to Ryder like a badly drawn f. He had assumed for two weeks that it was exactly that, some ancient printer's f for function, and he'd said so, once, out loud in class, and Ms. Nowak had not corrected him, had only said, interesting, and moved on, which had felt less like mercy than like a hook left in his mouth.

He reached for his phone, angling it away from Chelsey's view as if the search itself were a confession. The screen's glow through the diaphanous sheet of tracing paper she'd laid over the graph made the curve beneath it look doubled, ghosted. He read the result twice.

"It's an s," he said.

"What is?"

"The symbol. The long s. Gottfried Leibniz introduced it in 1675." He turned the phone so she could see. "He based it on an elongated letter s."

"An s for what?"

"Sum." Ryder said the word and felt it land somewhere behind his ribs, because it was the word Chelsey had used ten minutes ago without either of them knowing it was the word, the actual word, folded into the notation like a note passed across three centuries. "He thought of an integral as an infinite sum."

Chelsey leaned in, chewing the end of her pen. "So when Ms. Nowak writes it on the board, she's writing sum. Every single time."

"Every single time."

She sat back. "I liked it better as a mystery," she said, but she was already copying the curve onto her own paper, drawing the slices herself, and he watched her take it apart the way she took everything apart, first the outside, then the reason.

Ryder looked at the symbol again and found he had to give up something to keep it. The f had been wrong, and the wrongness had been comfortable, a shape he could dismiss; the s demanded that he believe infinitely many rectangles could be pressed into one clean number, and believing it was harder than memorizing it. He thought of Ms. Nowak saying interesting, and understood, with a small sour twinge, that she had left the door open on purpose, that she did this, that the class was mostly doors.

"Okay," he said. "Slices. Infinite sum." He pulled the tracing paper toward himself, sharpened his pencil against the table's edge, and beneath the doubled, ghostly curve began to draw rectangles so thin they were almost lines. Chelsey watched him, then uncapped a different pen, the red one she saved for arguments.

"If you get a different answer than me," she said, "we're not friends anymore."

"Then we're about to have a very long night."

He kept drawing, the rectangles marching out along the steppe of the page, each one narrower than the last, and outside the kitchen window a streetlamp came on, and neither of them looked up.

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: In his 1865 book The Coal Question, William Stanley Jevons observed that more efficient steam engines made coal cheaper to use and increased Britain's total coal consumption.
story:
The meter on the barn wall had begun to climb in the same month the town had declared its energy project a triumph. Antoine stood in front of it with his phone, photographing the readout the way his father photographed rain clouds, and behind him Damion dumped a bucket of feed into the trough and swore at the smell.

"Every house got the bulbs," Antoine said. "Everyone swapped over. So why is the co-op bill higher for the whole town than it was last summer?" Damion wiped his hands on his jeans and looked at the numbers as if they might rearrange themselves out of politeness. "Maybe more people moved in." "Four. Four houses. That's not this." The meter ticked upward while they watched it.

The farm was failing in the ordinary way farms failed, slowly and from several directions at once. His father had mortgaged the north field to put up the solar array three years ago, sanguine then about the payback period, telling the neighbours at the co-op meeting that sunlight was the one input nobody could repossess. What nobody had priced was the water. The aquifer had dropped, the pump ran longer, and longer pump hours meant higher draw from the grid on the grey weeks when the panels idled under haze. Antoine had begun to think that the farm's problems were not separate problems, that they were one problem wearing different hats, and the thought kept him awake in a way that felt almost useful.

He found the thing he needed in a used bookstore in town, on a shelf marked ECONOMICS, MUST GO. The Coal Question, 1865, William Stanley Jevons. He sat on the floor between the stacks with his knees up and read the passage twice, because the first time he was sure he had it backwards. More efficient steam engines had made coal cheaper to use, and Britain's total coal consumption had gone up. Efficiency had not shrunk the appetite. It had fed it.

Hanna was at the co-op office on Friday, arguing with the clerk about the billing tiers, and Antoine waited until she came out onto the step with her folder of printouts. "You were right that it wasn't the four new houses," she said. "I ran it. Usage per household stayed flat or fell. Total draw went up." "I know why," Antoine said. "Or I know a version of why. There was this economist, Jevons, 1865, The Coal Question. He watched more efficient steam engines make coal cheaper to use, and Britain's total coal consumption rose." Hanna frowned. "Steam engines." "Steam engines," Antoine agreed. "But if it worked then, it could work now. Cheap light, cheap heat, people stop being careful. It doesn't excuse us. It just means the bulbs were never the whole answer."

Hanna's detractors at the town council, and she had collected several by then, said she was chasing conspiracy. She said she was chasing arithmetic. The difference, she told Antoine on the step, was that arithmetic could be checked. "So check mine," he said. "The farm. Dad's panels. We save on power, the pump runs longer because the water's lower, the grid draw goes up on cloudy weeks, and the co-op raises the rates, and the rate raise makes Dad run the pump at night when it's cheaper, which drains the aquifer a little faster. I can't prove the last part. I don't have the well data." "Then we get the well data," Hanna said. "Mr. Kamau has it. He's been logging that aquifer for twenty years for nobody in particular."

Mr. Kamau lived at the property line where the county road bent, and he kept his records in a metal cabinet he had carried through three countries. He let Antoine copy the pages without commentary, watching him the whole time with an expression that contained, as far as Antoine could tell, no opinion at all. On the walk home the numbers in his notebook sat beside the numbers in his head, and he did the dishonest thing first, which was to look for a version of them where his father's panels had cost the town nothing. It wasn't there. The honest version was muddier: the array lowered some costs, raised others, and the sum depended on a water table he still couldn't see.

That night he laid the printouts on the kitchen table while his father ate standing at the counter. "The bulbs weren't wrong," Antoine said. "The bulbs were just bulbs." His father looked at the pages, then at him, and set down his fork. "What are you asking me for." "Nothing yet. I'm telling you what I found." Outside the window, the panels lay flat and black under the security light, and the light itself burned on a bulb the town had given them for free, efficient and bright and running all night, transmuting the co-op's coal into a small orange square on the grass.

His father came to the table and pulled a chair out with his foot. "Show me the well numbers first," he said. "Start there." Antoine turned to Mr. Kamau's pages, the pencil lines descending year over year like steps into a basement, and set his finger on the lowest one.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Supercompensation is the idea that the body gets fitter during recovery after training, when it rebuilds beyond its previous level, not during the workout itself.
story:
Kayla had been first into the gym every morning for three weeks, and she was getting slower. She noticed it on the third Tuesday, when her legs felt like she was jumping in a swimming pool, and she confirmed it on Friday, when Grady beat her in a layup drill for the first time since grade eight. The court behind the school sat near the riparian trail that ran along the creek, and she had started parking her bike down there so she could walk the last stretch and pretend the walk was a warm-up, which it wasn't, and she knew it wasn't.

"You look like a haunted couch," Katelynn said, watching her miss her fifth free throw in a row.

"I'm doing volume," Kayla said, as if volume were a currency and she were wealthy in it. "Coach says the ones who put in the hours are the ones who play."

"Coach also says the cafeteria pasta is 'nutrition,'" Katelynn said. "You've done something every single day for a month. Even Sunday."

"Sunday I only did two hundred shots."

"That's a rest day the way a paper cut is a surgery."

That night Kayla sat at the kitchen table with a legal pad, because planning things on legal pads made her feel like a lawyer, though the remuneration for varsity basketball was exactly zero dollars and a used water bottle. She had volunteered to build the team's off-season program as a project for Mr. Hassan's class, which had seemed like a way to make her obsession look academic. She wrote Monday through Sunday down the margin and then stopped, pen hovering, because she did not actually know what went in the boxes. She had never once written "rest" in a box in her life.

She texted Grady, who read actual books about training for reasons nobody understood.

Kayla: why am I slower. I train MORE than everyone.

Grady: ok so. you know how you get a blister and it heals into callus, thicker skin than before

Kayla: gross and irrelevant

Grady: it's called supercompensation. the body gets fitter during recovery after training, when it rebuilds beyond its previous level, not during the workout itself.

Kayla: that can't be right. you get better at basketball by playing basketball

Grady: you get better at basketball by playing basketball and then SLEEPING. I'm sending you a chapter. also you should probably problematize your whole "no days off" personality for your project, could be a strong thesis

She read the chapter twice, then read it a third time with the specific suspicion of someone being told the earth went around the sun. The idea insulted her. If fitness was built during recovery, then every 6 a.m. session she had added on top of the previous one was spending the rebuilding before it finished, like tearing up a road while the asphalt was still wet. She thought about her father, who had worked doubles for eleven years and called sick days a character flaw, and how she had absorbed that arithmetic without ever checking it. Maybe rest was not weakness wearing a costume. Maybe it was the actual work, happening somewhere she couldn't watch it. She wasn't sure. That was the part that bothered her most, that she couldn't watch it.

The next morning she took her notebook to the court by the creek and found Mr. Hassan already there, standing at the fence with his coffee, watching the mist come off the water.

"Your project proposal," he said. "Ambitious."

"I'm changing it," Kayla said. "I'm writing a weekly program. Hard days, easy days, warm-up before everything, and two rest days. Real ones."

"Two," he repeated, and she couldn't tell from his face whether he thought it was too many or too few, or whether his face just did that at six in the morning.

"Two," she said. "One after the hardest session, one later in the week. I'm testing it on myself for a month and timing everything, so I'll know if I'm wrong." She paused. "I might be wrong. I'm kind of hoping I'm not, because if I am, I've spent three weeks getting slower on purpose."

Mr. Hassan sipped his coffee. "That last sentence," he said, "is a better introduction than the one you handed in."

On Sunday, her first real rest day since September, Kayla rode her bike down to the riparian path anyway, because she didn't know how to be near the court without touching a ball. She sat on the railing with her notebook and watched the creek do whatever creeks did on their day off. Katelynn found her there at noon, holding two slushies.

"This is the rest day?" Katelynn said, handing her one. "You look like you're guarding the water."

"I'm observing recovery," Kayla said. "It's research."

"It's a creek."

Ten days later, on the Thursday session, Kayla beat Grady in the layup drill by two full lengths, then beat him again, then stood at the free throw line breathing hard and not saying anything, because saying something would have been unbearable to them both. Grady retrieved the ball, spun it on one finger, and looked at her with a squint.

"One data point," he said.

"Nine days of data points," she said, and took the ball back.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: Andrew Wakefield's 1998 Lancet paper claiming a link between the MMR vaccine and autism described just twelve children, and The Lancet fully retracted it in 2010.
story:
Amy's aunt had pressed the printout into her hand in the pediatrician's waiting room, the paper still warm from her bag, and said, "Read this before you let them give your cousin the second shot." The article was old, older than Amy, and it mentioned a study in a journal called The Lancet that had found a link between the MMR vaccine and autism. Amy had folded it into her backpack without agreeing to anything, and the folding, she understood even then, was its own kind of answer.

Two days later she was at the library with Tom, who was nominally working on a history paper about a municipal ordinance that had segregated his town's swimming pools in the 1930s. He had three books open and was copying citations into a legal pad. Amy set the printout on the table between them. "Do you know anything about this?" she asked. Tom read the first paragraph, then the last, then turned the page over as if the back might contain a disclaimer. "My mom's a nurse," he said. "She'd have opinions." He didn't say what the opinions were, which Amy took to mean he didn't want to be the one to deliver them.

She went looking on her own. The library's databases were stricter than her phone, which served her whatever she seemed to want, and she liked that about them. She found the original 1998 paper first, or the shape of it: a description of twelve children. Twelve. She sat back in the chair and looked at that number for a while. Twelve children, and she had heard the article's claim repeated her whole life as though it were a verdict on millions.

Then she found the rest. In 2010, The Lancet had fully retracted the paper. She read the word "retracted" three times. It wasn't a correction, and it wasn't a follow-up; it was the journal pulling the whole thing back, the way a store pulls a product from shelves. When she said the sentence out loud in a murmur, the girl at the next carrel glanced over, and Amy mouthed sorry.

Mr. Shapiro, the reference librarian, came by with a cart of returns and noticed her screen. "Going deep," he said. She asked him whether a retraction meant the finding had been proven false, and he tilted his head the way he did when a question deserved a better question. "What do you think it takes before a lot of scientists agree on something?" he said. "One paper? Two?" Then he pushed the cart on toward the biography section, and Amy understood he was leaving the answer to her, which was annoying and, later, something she was grateful for.

She spent another hour chasing the trail: other researchers who had looked at the same question, larger groups of children, journals where work was read by other scientists before it was published. None of it felt like a single dramatic reveal. It felt like weight accumulating on one side of a scale, study after study, until the scale itself became the evidence. That was the part she hadn't expected. She had imagined truth arriving the way it did in movies, in a flash, and instead it arrived like Tom's legal pad, line after line of citations, each one leaning on the ones before it.

Valeria found her at the table near closing, sliding into the chair Tom had vacated, stealing a pretzel from the open bag. Amy told her about the aunt, the waiting room, the twelve children, the retraction, the way consensus seemed to form not from one voice but from a chorus checking each other. Valeria listened with her chin in her hand. "So what are you going to tell your aunt?" Amy said she didn't know yet. Her aunt wasn't stupid, and Amy didn't want to walk in armed with a lecture, because lectures had never changed anyone's mind in that family. But she also couldn't fold the truth into her backpack the way she'd folded the article. Her plan was still inchoate, more of an intention than a strategy, and she said so.

The overhead lights clicked to half, the signal Mr. Shapiro gave ten minutes before the doors locked. Valeria gathered the pretzel bag and Amy's pens while Amy printed one page, just one, the retraction notice itself, its thin ink still warm when she took it from the tray. Outside, the parking lot was dark except for one sodium lamp over the entrance, moths ticking against the glass. Amy folded the page once, lengthwise, and put it in her pocket, where she could feel the edge of it against her hip the whole walk to the car. "Text me after you talk to her," Valeria said, unlocking the doors. "Whatever she says, I want to hear it."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: India has marked voters' fingers with indelible ink based on silver nitrate since its 1962 general election, so no one can vote twice.
story:
Mr. Shevchenko had arranged the desks in a horseshoe and taped a cardboard sign above the radiator that read POLLING STATION. On Monday Mya would turn eighteen, and on Tuesday the actual polling station at the middle school gym would open at seven in the morning. Mr. Shevchenko knew this because she had told him, twice, once in September and once last week when she asked whether the class could stage a mock vote so she would know what to expect.

"You'll mark a paper ballot, fold it, and slide it into the box," he said. "Then an officer will mark the register beside your name. That's the whole ceremony." Mohamed-Amine raised his hand and asked what stopped someone from voting twice, and Mr. Shevchenko shrugged and said that here it was mostly the register, and the honesty of the poll workers who remembered faces, and that Mya could research it for the class if she wanted extra credit. Mya said she would think about it. She did not demur for the credit; she demured because the question was the first interesting one anyone had asked all term.

That night she found her aunt's photo album from the year she had gone back to Pune for the winter. Toward the back there was a picture of her cousin Priya standing outside a school, holding up her right index finger for the camera. The finger was stained a deep purple-black from the nail to the first knuckle. Mya texted Priya, who replied four hours later because of the time difference: it was indelible ink, and everyone who voted got marked so no one could vote twice. Priya added that India had done it since the 1962 general election, with ink based on silver nitrate, and that she had kept the stain as long as she could, out of pride, before scrubbing it off.

Mya sat with the photo on her screen for a while. Priya had voted at nineteen, in a country where her one vote was one among hundreds of millions, and the mark on her finger had been the entire proof of it. In the gym on Tuesday there would be no mark. There would only be a name in a binder and a folded paper, and then Mya would walk out indistinguishable from anyone who had not voted at all. She copied Priya's messages into her notes and closed the laptop.

On Thursday the class held its mock election for student council treasurer. Mya had brought a bottle of ink from the art room, the kind that stained skin for days, and she set it on the table beside the shoebox they were using as a ballot box. Gibson, who was working the table as a poll officer, looked at the bottle and then at her. "We're supposed to check names off the list," he said. "That's the system."

"The list can be wrong," Mya said. "A name gets missed, or someone votes for someone else. In India they mark your finger with indelible ink, silver nitrate based, since their 1962 general election, so nobody can vote twice." She held up the photo of Priya, printed that morning in the library for fifteen cents. Gibson studied it, and Mohamed-Amine leaned across two desks to look, and for a minute the line at the table stopped being a line and became a cluster of people looking at one purple finger.

"It's a good system," Mohamed-Amine said. "But it assumes nobody votes twice because they can't, not because they chose not to." Mr. Shevchenko, who had been pretending to grade papers at his desk, said that this was the oldest argument in the field, and that Mya had just walked them into the middle of it without a map. He asked the class which they would rather rely on, a stain or a promise. Gibson said the stain, obviously. Mohamed-Amine said obviously nothing, that a system built only on preventing the worst in people might end up expecting it, and Mya heard in that an echo of something her father had said at dinner, though he had said it about locked gates and she had argued the other side then.

She thought about teleology for the rest of the period, a word she had learned in this same room during a unit on Aristotle that she had assumed she would never use. If the purpose of an election was only the count, then the ink was perfect and the register was a sloppy cousin. But if the purpose included the walk to the gym, the line, the small public act of being seen to choose, then the mark did something the register could not: it let Priya carry her vote out of the school on her hand, visible for days. Mya's father would call that sentimental. She herself was not sure whether it was sentimental or simply a different accounting of what a vote was for.

They compromised for the rest of the mock election. Gibson kept the register, and Mya dabbed ink onto the tip of each voter's finger with a cotton swab, and eleven of fourteen students agreed to it, one of them, a boy who claimed a congenital aversion to having his hands touched, asking to initial the register twice instead. When the bell rang the ballots were counted on the windowsill and Mohamed-Amine won by three votes, and the ink was still on Mya's own fingertip from when she had demonstrated on herself.

At the gym on Tuesday morning Mya gave her name, took the ballot, and slid it into the box. On her way out she stopped at the table where an older woman sat with the register and a roll of stickers that read I VOTED. The woman offered one, and Mya looked at it, a small round flag with adhesive on the back, and asked, "Do you have anything that lasts longer?"

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: The Sabbath commandment appears twice in the Hebrew Bible with different reasons: Exodus 20 cites God resting after creation, while Deuteronomy 5 cites Israel's release from slavery in Egypt.
story:
Chase had the whole commandment memorized, or close enough, which was why he'd told Nigel he didn't need to bring the Bible to the cemetery. They were meeting Sebastien by the gates at four, an hour before the debate team's practice argument, because Sebastien's grandmother was buried here and he liked to do his flashcards near her headstone, and Nigel liked anywhere with shade. Chase had claimed, with some confidence, that the Sabbath commandment appeared once, in Exodus, and that the reason for it was obvious: God rested after creation, so you rest too. Case closed. He'd even said "case closed" out loud, walking up the hill, which was the kind of thing he said when he hadn't yet opened the book.

"You're sure it's only in Exodus once?" Nigel asked, because Nigel had a habit of asking the one question that mattered and then looking at the grass.

"Two and two," Chase said, meaning fourth commandment, two tablets. He wasn't entirely sure what he meant, but it sounded like knowing.

They found Sebastien on the bench beside his grandmother's stone, a fat paperback open on his knee, and he didn't even look up. "Deuteronomy," he said.

"What?"

"You're wrong. It's in Deuteronomy too. Chapter five. And it doesn't say anything about creation." Sebastien turned the book around, and Chase took it, and the afternoon went quiet in the way it does in cemeteries, as if the grass were listening.

He read it twice. Remember the Sabbath day. Same opening. Same command to keep it holy. But then the reason underneath the rule was different, a different floor beneath the same house. Deuteronomy said to remember that you were a slave in Egypt, and that God brought you out with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, and therefore the Lord commanded you to keep the Sabbath day. Not rest after creation. Release from slavery. Chase sat down on the bench without deciding to. The commandment had always seemed like one solid thing to him, like a headstone, and now it had two reasons carved under it, and the two reasons didn't match. Was the Sabbath about imitating God, or about giving your workers and your animals a day no one could take from them, because you once had everything taken from you? Which one was the real reason, or were both real, or did real even apply to a text this old? The questions arrived the way birds arrive at a feeder, all at once and jostling.

"You look mesmerized," Nigel said. "It's not that mesmerizing."

"It kind of is," Chase said, still reading. "If the reason changes, then what we're arguing about in the debate changes. Like, if it's about creation, then it's about rhythm, about being a creature. If it's about Egypt, it's about power. About not being a Pharaoh to your own employees."

From the next row of stones, where she had been deadheading the roses along the low fence, Ms. Cardinal had heard most of this, though she would later tell her sister she'd heard all of it, which was her way. She was retired from teaching humanities at the community college, and she found the whole scene faintly funny: three boys with a paperback Bible on a grave bench, arguing scripture while a lawnmower droned somewhere behind the spruces. She did not believe in marching over to explain things to young people; she had done that for thirty-one years and had mostly learned that they remembered what they found themselves. So she only said, as she carried her bucket past, "There's a word for what you're doing, you know. Reading the text against the text. Hermeneutics."

Sebastien mouthed the word back at her. Chase wrote it on his hand in pen.

"It's not a cheat code," she called over her shoulder. "It's a discipline. The ancillary question is always whether the rule survives its reasons."

Chase looked at the two chapters, laid open across his knee and Nigel's. He could build his debate position on both reasons at once, he thought; he could say the commandment persists because both floors hold, one about the shape of a week and one about the dignity of the powerless, and that a rule with two reasons in two books is probably a rule that means more than either reason alone. Or he could admit, standing at the podium, that he didn't know which reason the rule leaned on, and argue from the not knowing. That felt more honest and harder. He tried out a first line under his breath. Nigel threw a pinecone at him.

"Save it for practice," Nigel said. "You're doing the podium voice."

"That is not a podium voice. That's my thinking voice."

Sebastien closed his grandmother's Bible, gently, the way you close something borrowed, and put his hand flat on the cover. "Same words at the top," he said. "Different story underneath. That's going to be my opening line, actually."

"You can't take it, I found it," Chase said, and reached for the book, and Sebastien held it out of reach over the roses.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: K. Anders Ericsson and colleagues' 1993 study of violinists described 'deliberate practice': effortful work on specific weaknesses with immediate feedback, not just logging hours.
story:
Felix chalked two lines into the dry grass with his heel, ten yards apart, and set down the orange cones he'd carried over in a milk crate. The backyard belonged to his mother, but on Saturday mornings between eight and nine it belonged to him, and to the seven ten-year-olds who arrived on bikes with their shin guards already on. He had two weeks until the league's spring season started, two weeks to fix a passing game that had spent the whole winter falling apart.

The weakness was specific. He had watched the scrimmages his friend Isaiah filmed in February, all forty minutes of them, and counted. The kids could trap a ball and they could kick a ball, but the moment a pass needed to travel more than five yards, it either died halfway or skidded out of bounds. They never practiced passing as a thing in itself. They just played games, every single practice, and logged the hours and stayed exactly as bad as they'd been in November.

"It's like those violin people," Isaiah said, sitting on the back step with the crate of spare balls between his feet. He'd read it for a psychology elective and would not stop bringing it up. "Ericsson, 1993. They called it deliberate practice. Effortful work on one specific weakness with feedback right away, not just piling up hours."

"You've said that four times."

"Because it's true four times."

Felix ignored him, mostly. He had his own version of it anyway, one that fit into a backyard: a drill where a pass that died short meant the passer ran to retrieve it, and where Felix called out, within two seconds, what the leg had done wrong. Locked ankle. Eyes on the receiver, not the ball. The kids would hate it, he suspected, because it wasn't a game, and games were the only thing they'd ever been offered.

Lena arrived at eight-fifteen with her clipboard, because Lena arrived everywhere with a clipboard. She was the assistant Felix had been assigned, though nobody had explained to either of them what an assistant to a sixteen-year-old was supposed to do. She watched him explain the drill, watched the first pair go, watched the ball die in the grass a yard short of the target cone, and Felix made the kid retrieve it and said, "Locked ankle, Marco, the ankle," and the second pass arrived clean and low and the small boy at the cone trapped it without stumbling.

"They're getting feedback inside two seconds," Lena said, in a voice like she was reading off the clipboard.

"That's the point."

"And they hate it."

"That's also the point." He didn't fully believe that. He believed it about half, and the other half was watching a boy named Kwame, the best player of the seven, standing at the end of the line with his arms crossed, because Kwame was good at scrimmages and drills were a place where being good at scrimmages bought you nothing. That was the thing Felix hadn't solved yet: how to make the boring work bearable without turning it back into the game that had failed them all winter.

What he hadn't told anyone, not Isaiah, not Lena, was that Mr. Guo was on his porch. He lived two houses down and his fence backed onto the yard, and he was out there with his coffee at eight-thirty in the cold, saying nothing, watching. And Mr. Guo, though the kids didn't know it and Isaiah had never asked, was the one who ran the league's youth development committee, the one who had taken a chance on a sixteen-year-old head coach and would decide in June whether that had been a mistake.

"Is it genetic?" Lena asked, mostly to be annoying. "Some kids just can't pass?"

"It's not phenotypic," Isaiah said from the step. "It's not written in them. Nobody's born unable to hit a ten-yard ball."

"It's habit," Felix said. "You can resuscitate a flat pass, you just have to catch it before it leaves the foot." He said it louder than he needed to, and he knew why, and he was embarrassed to know why: he was performing for the porch.

The drill ran twelve minutes. Seven kids, maybe eighty passes, and Felix counted the clean ones against the dead ones in his head. At the start it had been one in three. By the last rotation it was closer to one in two, and one boy who had never completed a pass all winter hit the cone twice in a row and looked around to see whether anyone had registered it. Felix registered it. He put his hand flat on the top of his head, the signal for good, and the boy did it back.

Then Kwame broke the line. He collected a dead ball, and instead of jogging it back he pivoted and hit a forty-yard cross-field pass, gorgeous and arrogant, that dropped out of the sky onto the trampoline and rolled off into the flowerbed. Everyone laughed. Felix felt the drill dissolving, the whole structure, twelve minutes of ankles and feedback, and he had a choice, and he understood it was a real one: punish it and protect the work, or let it go and protect the player.

He looked at the porch. Mr. Guo was standing now, mug in hand, still saying nothing.

"Kwame," Felix called. "That was the best pass all morning."

Kwame straightened up, caught off guard by kindness.

"It was also the wrong pass, and it's in the flowers. Bring it back and hit the cone from ten yards like everyone else, and when practice ends, I want to see it again from forty." Felix turned to the line. "From the top."

The first pair stepped up. On the porch, Mr. Guo set his mug down on the rail.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and guanine pairs with cytosine; in RNA, uracil takes the place of thymine and pairs with adenine.
story:
The pond behind the school had one bench that faced the water and one that faced the parking lot, and Jayden had learned by now to take the one facing the water, because otherwise he watched cars instead of thinking. He spread his biology notebook across his knees. On the page was a DNA sequence Mr. Nikolaidis had written on the board that morning, and beneath it, half finished, the RNA Jayden was supposed to produce from it. Somewhere after that came a chain of amino acids, a protein, the thing the whole assignment was secretly about. He wrote slowly, mouthing the pairings to himself. Adenine with thymine, guanine with cytosine. That part felt solid, like multiplication he'd known since he was small.

"Are you actually doing homework out here?" Noor dropped onto the grass beside the bench with her own bag, having walked the path from the library, where the windows faced the wrong direction for her liking. She claimed the pond was a better milieu for studying than any building, though Jayden suspected she mostly liked watching the ducks argue over bread. "Move over. I'm stuck on the same sheet."

They compared answers. Her DNA strand matched his. Her RNA matched his too, which was comforting until it wasn't, because both of them had written T, thymine, all the way through the RNA copy, wherever adenine appeared in the original. Jayden stared at his own handwriting. Something about it bothered him the way a word looks wrong after you've written it ten times.

"Wait," he said. "Is RNA even supposed to have thymine in it?"

Noor demurred, not out of politeness but out of genuine uncertainty; she pulled her phone out, then put it face down on the grass without checking it, because she wanted to reason it through first. "There were four letters on the board for RNA. I remember four. A, C, G, and something else."

Jayden flipped back two pages in his notes, to Tuesday, when he'd been half asleep and drawing duck shapes in the margin. There it was in his own rushed hand: in RNA, uracil takes the place of thymine. He read it twice. "Uracil," he said aloud, and the word felt new in his mouth, like a name he'd heard once at a party. So when the DNA had adenine, the RNA didn't answer with thymine at all. It answered with uracil. The same pairs otherwise, adenine and guanine and cytosine doing what they'd always done, but one letter swapped out, as if the copy were made by a scribe with one stubborn quirk.

"That's it," Noor said. "That's why mine looked weird. Every T should be a U." She began correcting her sheet with sharp little strokes of her pen, and Jayden did the same, crossing out each thymine he'd wrongly carried over, until the page looked like a letter written in a storm. He noticed, as he worked, that he liked the correction more than he would have liked getting it right the first time. The mistake had made the difference visible. A copy that was identical wouldn't need its own vocabulary.

Karen arrived last, headphones around her neck, and leaned over the bench to see what they were doing. "You're still on the transcription part? I finished at lunch." Her tone had an acerbic edge, but she sat down anyway, close enough that Jayden could smell the chlorine still in her hair from morning practice. When she looked at their corrected pages, her eyebrows went up. "Oh. I wrote T everywhere too."

"Everyone writes T," Jayden said. "It's the natural mistake. Your hand wants to copy."

The three of them worked forward together then, translating the corrected RNA into its amino acids using the chart in the back of the book, and Jayden found himself explaining it out loud, pointing at each three-letter group as he went, which was strange, because explaining it made it clearer in his own head than reading it ever had. He still couldn't have said why uracil and not thymine, why the cell kept two alphabets instead of one, and he said so, and Noor shrugged and said maybe nobody in the class could, maybe that was just the next door down the hall. The ducks had gone quiet. The water was flattening out into evening, holding the last of the light.

Jayden read his final protein chain against the answer Noor had produced independently, letter by letter, and they matched, and he sat back and looked at the pond rather than at the page, at the rings spreading from where some insect had touched the surface. He wondered whether every small correction in the world felt like this, one letter changed and the whole sentence suddenly meaning something.

"Same time tomorrow?" Karen said, capping her pen.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In a 1966 experiment by Elliot Aronson and colleagues, a highly competent quiz contestant who spilled a cup of coffee was rated more likable afterward; this is called the pratfall effect.
story:
Laurie had rehearsed the walk from the bus stop to the fountain exactly twice, once with Khloe and once alone, and both times the mall had seemed smaller, less humid, less loud with its ceiling fans turning the smell of cinnamon pretzels through the food court like weather. Tonight the escalators gleamed and everything smelled like popcorn butter, and she kept touching her collar as though confirming she was still the person who had chosen this shirt an hour ago. Jaxon was already waiting by the fountain, and when he waved she felt the whole biome of the mall shift around her, shoppers and pigeons-of-people orbiting the one fixed point that mattered.

He bought them both lemonades at the stand near the arcade, and he was funny in the way she remembered from chemistry class, quick and a little acerbic, making dry remarks about a poster for a cell phone company. She laughed twice before they had even sat down. Then, reaching for napkins, his elbow caught his cup, and lemonade went across the table and into his lap, and ice skittered onto the floor and under the shoe of a passing toddler, whose mother gave them a look of ancient disappointment.

"It's fine," Laurie said, already wiping, but Jaxon had gone very still. "Honestly, it's the table's fault, it wobbles."

"I just ruined it," he said. "The whole first five minutes. You're going to go home and tell Khloe I'm the guy who wears his drink."

She had been about to say something reassuring and automatic, but instead she heard herself say, "Wait. Khloe told me about this exact thing." She reached for the story carefully, the way you reach for a glass in the dark. "There was this experiment in 1966, by a guy named Elliot Aronson and some other researchers. They had a quiz contestant, someone really competent, and the contestant spills a cup of coffee. Afterward people rated him more likable. Not less. More."

Jaxon looked at her with lemonade still darkening the knee of his jeans. "You made that up to be nice."

"I didn't. It's called the pratfall effect. Khloe's taking a psych course at the community college and she talks about it constantly." She hadn't actually believed she would ever use the fact; it had seemed like trivia, a coin she kept in a drawer. But here it was, spendable.

He mopped at the table with the last dry napkin, considering. "So if I'd been boring and then spilled, no bonus."

She hadn't thought about that part. Was the effect about competence, then, about a fall only counting if you had somewhere to fall from? She wondered whether that was fair, whether a klutz got abrogated of the benefit entirely, or whether everyone had enough competence somewhere in them to qualify. She didn't say any of this out loud, because she was aware that thinking it was more interesting than announcing it, and because she liked discovering she could hold a question without demanding it resolve.

"That's the theory, I think," she said. "I only know what Khloe told me."

They walked after that, past the window of a shoe store where a mannequin leaned against nothing, past Mr. Yamamoto from her biology class, who taught one building over, nodding at her with mild surprise, and she waved and did not stop. She and Jaxon argued companionably about whether the mall aquarium store's octopus was real, and she noticed that his funny remarks had softened, that the dryness now included himself in its aim. Was that the coffee doing its work, or was he just relaxing? She couldn't separate the two, and the not-knowing felt less like a failure than like the beginning of how you got to know anyone.

At the fountain again, an hour and a half later, he said, "For the record, I'm glad I spilled."

"You're citing the study."

"I'm an anecdote," he said. "One data point." He picked a piece of ice out of the fountain's rim, left over from nothing, impossible, and dropped it back in.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: For Mexico's Day of the Dead on November 1 and 2, families build home altars called ofrendas with orange marigolds, whose bright color and strong scent are believed to guide souls home.
story:
The church hall smelled of wax and pan dulce, and along the far wall someone had set up a long table covered in purple paper. Gabriella held her grandmother's photograph against her chest and watched the families ahead of hers move down the line, arranging sugar skulls and candles and food on the altars they had built. Her mother nudged her forward.

The altar was not like the one at home. At home they had assembled it on the credenza in the hallway: two framed photos, a small dish of her grandmother's favorite guava candies, a cross made of salt. Here the parish had invited families to add photographs to a communal ofrenda for the celebration on the first and second of November, and Ms. Chatterjee, who taught world religions at the high school and had helped organize it, stood at the end of the table greeting each family in turn.

"You brought her," Ms. Chatterjee said, and her voice softened around the photograph. "Set her wherever there's room."

Gabriella looked for room and found the problem. Every altar, every family's arrangement, had marigolds. Rows of them, orange as embers, fresh ones and papery dried ones, scattered in loose arcs around the frames. Her family's section had none. Her mother had sent her out the door early with the photograph and a bag of candles, assuming the flowers were already handled; the flowers had not been handled; and now her grandmother's picture sat on purple paper with nothing around it but a candle stub someone else had left. She knew the flowers mattered. Her grandmother, in the last autumn of her life, had stood at the sink rinsing marigold petals while Gabriella dried dishes, and had said, without looking up, that the altar was called an ofrenda and that on the first and second of November the souls came home along the scent. Gabriella had been twelve and had asked how a soul could smell anything, and her grandmother had laughed and said the bright color helped too, like a lamp left in a window. She had not thought about that afternoon in four years, and now it returned to her entire, the wet orange smell of the sink, her grandmother's wrists thin above the basin.

She texted Alexanne and Lauren, who were both at the celebration somewhere, and then found them near the punch. "I need marigolds," she said. "Before my mom notices. She'll feel terrible."

"Where do we get marigolds at seven at night?" Lauren asked.

"Ms. Chatterjee's garden. She told our class she grows them, she had some tangential story about it when we were supposed to be reviewing for the exam." Alexanne was already pulling her jacket on. "Her street is two blocks over. She lives alone, she'll be home in an hour when the blessing starts."

The three of them found Ms. Chatterjee's house dark at the windows and knocked anyway, and when she opened the door in reading glasses she did not seem surprised to see them. "For the ofrenda," Gabriella said, and hated how the request adumbrated the whole afternoon, her carelessness, her mother's grief. Ms. Chatterjee went into the cold yard with a flashlight and came back with her arms full, and she did not make a speech about it, only said, "Cut them long, there's more where that came from," and closed the door.

They ran the two blocks carrying the flowers against their chests, and the cold made the scent sharper, and Gabriella thought that if the smell really did lead anyone anywhere then surely it was doing its work right now, across the dark yards, along the sidewalk. She did not believe it exactly. She could not have said what she believed. But her grandmother had believed it, had rinsed the petals with her own hands believing it, and placing the flowers seemed less like making a claim about souls and more like keeping faith with the woman who had made the claim first.

At the hall, her mother was still near the front, listening to the priest begin a long peroration about remembrance, and she did not see them. Gabriella laid the marigolds in an arc around the photograph, close enough that the petals touched the frame, and stepped back beside Alexanne and Lauren in the dim orange candlelight. The flowers were already filling the air above the altar, and the first family in line was leaning forward to light a candle for their own.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Kintsugi is a Japanese technique of repairing broken pottery with lacquer mixed or dusted with powdered gold, treating the break as part of the object's history rather than hiding it.
story:
Cohen had told his mother the bowl was safe on the shelf, and for three days that had even been true, which was why he kept telling it to himself as though repetition could retroact it into fact. What had actually happened was simpler and worse: he had been reaching past it for his grandfather's chess book, his elbow had caught the rim, and the bowl, a blue-glazed thing his grandfather had carried home from Okinawa decades before Cohen was born, had struck the floor and split into four clean pieces and a scatter of smaller ones. He had swept them into a shoebox before his mother came home. Now it was Friday, and she had announced over breakfast that she wanted to photograph the bowl for the family history project on Sunday, which gave him approximately forty hours.

The art room after last period was where he went instead of home, because the art room had a drying cabinet, a wall of glues and epoxies Mr. Bui kept behind a labeled cabinet, and, crucially, Karlee, who was sanding a plaster cast of her own hand and did not look up when he set the shoebox on her table.

"You look like someone who prognosticated badly," she said, blowing plaster dust off her knuckles. "Like you saw the future and it was this face."

"I need glue that fixes ceramics so you can't see the seam." He opened the box. Karlee stopped sanding.

"Oh, Cohen." She picked up the largest piece and turned it in the light of the window, and even Cohen, who had spent three days constructing the argument that a repaired bowl was still the bowl, felt the argument wobble. The break was jagged, mineral-white against the blue. "She's going to see it from across the room."

"That's why the seam has to vanish."

Sebastian arrived the way he always did, already mid-sentence, carrying two sodas and a rumor about the tennis coach. He put both sodas down when he saw the pieces. "That's the Okinawa bowl. The one your mom won't let anyone touch at Thanksgiving. Cohen, you are so dead."

"Thank you."

"Unless," Sebastian said, and then he went quiet in the way that meant he was genuinely thinking rather than performing it, "you don't hide it."

Mr. Bui had come out of the supply closet with a jar of gold mica powder in one hand, and whether he had heard any of this Cohen could not say, because Mr. Bui's face was reliably noncommittal, a face that withheld judgment the way a locked cabinet withheld glue. He set the jar on the table between them. "I'm running the kiln until six," he said, which answered a question none of them had asked aloud, and went back into the closet.

Karlee turned the jar in her fingers. "Kintsugi," she said, and when Cohen's expression stayed blank, she made it simpler: "the Japanese way of repairing broken pottery with lacquer mixed with gold. The break is supposed to show."

"Show," Cohen repeated. He was aware of a small internal collision, the part of him that wanted the seam invisible running into the part that had, last spring, written a college essay about how his grandfather's stories never hid their rough years, and he did not enjoy noticing the collision. "That's insane."

"It's not hiding the history," Sebastian said. "It's like the opposite."

They had until Sunday, which was not enough time for real lacquer, which cured for weeks; they had, instead, an epoxy that set in an hour and the jar of mica. Karlee held the pieces while Cohen ran a bead of the mixed gold along each edge, his hands steadier than he expected, and Sebastian read aloud from his phone about the technique and mispronounced everything with such confidence that Karlee began grading his elocution out of ten. Two of the four large pieces fit almost perfectly. One had lost a chip the size of a fingernail, and the smallest fragment had crumbled past saving, so there was a gap, and this was the part Cohen turned over and over while the epoxy cured in the cabinet's warmth: the bowl could not be what it had been, and the gold made no claim that it could. It drew a bright line along every failure and called that a finish.

He took it out at five-thirty, when the light through the west windows went long and orange. The gold seams caught it and lit up like something deliberately planned, like rivers on a map of a country that had been through something. His mother would see them from across the room. There was no version of Sunday in which she did not see them. He was not sure whether the bowl he would hand her was a lie or the truth, or whether those were even the available options, and he suspected the honest answer was that he did not get to decide in advance what she would see.

Sebastian leaned over his shoulder. "So do we prognosticate your survival, or?"

"Noncommittal," Cohen said, and turned the bowl once more in the light.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: Eye-contact norms differ: steady eye contact often signals confidence in North American interviews, while in some East Asian settings prolonged direct gaze at a senior person can seem impolite.
story:
Jaxon's mother straightened his collar in the kitchen, frowning at the laptop balanced on a stack of cookbooks. "Remember what I told you," she said. "Look down sometimes. At my old office in Seoul, a boy who stared at the manager would be considered rude."

An hour later his uncle Marcus called from the driveway, phone propped against the steering wheel, and said the opposite. "Steady eye contact, Jax. That's the whole game. Managers here read it as confidence." He made Jaxon practice on the video call, holding his gaze until Jaxon's face went hot. "You'll desensitize," Marcus said cheerfully. "Twenty more seconds."

Between the two of them, Jaxon felt like a compass near two magnets. He retreated to his room, where Flora was sprawled on the carpet with the practice questions Ms. Bekele had printed for him. She read one aloud, florid and formal, about overcoming challenges, and he answered while trying to look at her the way Marcus wanted. She started laughing before he finished.

"You look like you're arresting me," she said.

He tried again, softer, dropping his eyes the way his mother wanted, and Flora said he looked like he was hiding something. He sat back against the bed. It wasn't that either of them was wrong. His mother had worked in offices in Seoul; Marcus had interviewed people in this city for fifteen years. Both of them had watched real hiring happen. The trouble was that they were describing two different rooms.

"So which one is the interview in?" Flora asked. She had a way of cutting to the thing he was circling. Jaxon scrolled through the email from the hardware store. The manager's name was Yuki Sato. He didn't know what that meant, or whether it meant anything. He texted Violette, whose family ran the flower shop next to the hardware store, and she wrote back within a minute: "Ms. Sato? She's from Osaka. She hired my cousin. Super nice. Why?"

Jaxon stared at the message. His mother's advice had come from a specific place, and Ms. Sato had come from a specific place too, and neither of those places was this kitchen, where Flora was now eating his emergency granola bars. It occurred to him that he could not actually solve this with causality, the way you could solve a physics problem, where the same input always produces the same output. Person A plus eye contact did not equal judgment B. Ms. Sato had been hiring in this city for years, at a store where the customers called her by her first name; maybe she had already adapted. Or maybe some habits went deeper than geography. He genuinely did not know, and there was something almost freeing in admitting that, though it was also the worst possible timing.

"So what are you going to do?" Flora asked, brushing crumbs off her jeans.

"A middle thing," Jaxon said. "Eye contact when I answer, eyes down when she talks. Like I'm listening hard instead of challenging her."

"That's not a plan, that's a compromise."

"It's both."

The interview was the next afternoon, webcam set up on the same stack of cookbooks while his mother hovered out of frame. Ms. Sato appeared on screen in a store apron, shelves of paint cans behind her. Jaxon kept his eyes on hers while he spoke about restocking shelves and customer service, then lowered them, once, deliberately, when she described the Saturday morning rush. She paused, and he could not read the pause at all, and then she smiled and said he'd hear back by Friday.

His mother, who had watched the whole thing from the doorway, said nothing on the drive to Flora's house, nothing while he ate, nothing until he was half out of the car. "You looked respectful," she said finally. "Not weak. There's a difference."

He was still holding his phone when the message arrived, two days early: Could you start Saturday? He read it twice, then looked up at the porch light, at his mother's taillights turning the corner, at the door where Flora was already asking to see.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: The First Amendment limits what the government can do to speech; it does not by itself stop a private employer or private company from restricting speech.
story:
Savannah had claimed the carrel by the window on the third floor of the public library, the one with the wobble in its left leg, because the wobble kept her awake. Spread before her were the packet for the mock Supreme Court, a printout of the fictional case, and her own handwriting spiraling into the margin: violating free speech rights, private website, deleted account. She had chosen to argue that a student's First Amendment rights were violated when a private website deleted his posts, and she had been proud of the choice for exactly one day.

Andrew dropped his backpack on the table across from her. "I drew the other side," he said. "You know that, right?" He slid a granola bar across the wood like a peace offering, and she took it without answering, because answering would have meant admitting she had written her first paragraph as though the First Amendment applied to everyone, to every forum, to any company with a logo and a report button.

"You're going to preempt me in rebuttal," she said. "You'll say the whole case is moot." He didn't deny it. He peeled the wrapper back slowly, an aesthete about even cheap granola, and she flipped her pages face down so he couldn't read them.

They worked in parallel for an hour. When he left for his shift at the grocery store, she went to the reference desk and asked Ms. Pierre for anything on First Amendment doctrine, expecting a thick book with a cracked spine. Ms. Pierre set down a slim volume and a photocopy of a plain-language summary, and said only, "Start here, then tell me what you find." Savannah read the summary twice at the window while the sun moved off the parking lot, and the sentence she had skipped past a dozen times finally stood still long enough for her to see it. The First Amendment limits what the government can do to speech; it does not by itself stop a private employer or private company from restricting speech. She looked up at the parking lot, at the county courthouse dome two blocks east, and understood that she had been aiming her argument at the wrong building entirely.

She texted Nadine, who was arguing the same side at a different school: "Our case is dead, right? The website is private. The First Amendment doesn't reach it." Then, before Nadine could reply, she added, "Unless I argue the website acted at the government's request. There's nothing like that in the facts. I checked twice."

From Nadine's side of the conversation, sitting on her bedroom floor with the case packet open and the phone balanced on her knee, the message looked like surrender dressed up as a question. She typed back: "My coach says to concede it and build the case on values instead. Free speech as a principle, not an amendment. Is that honest or is it a dodge?" She stared at what she had written, thinking of last year, when she had stayed quiet in a class discussion she later regretted missing, and whether that memory was actually germane to anything or just a story she told herself to feel like someone who cared about speech at all. She sent it anyway.

Savannah read the reply in the library lobby, under the hum of the vending machine. She thought about her brother, who had been fired from a warehouse job the summer before for what he said in the break room, and how everyone in the family had said "free speech" as if it were a shield he had simply failed to raise, when what had happened was that the shield did not cover that ground at all. She wrote back: "It's honest if we say the amendment stops at the government's edge and then ask what should happen beyond it. Different question. We shouldn't pretend it's the same one."

The next afternoon she rewrote her opening argument at the wobbly table. She conceded the doctrine in her first minute, plainly, the way Ms. Pierre had declined to explain anything and simply pointed. Then she spent her remaining four minutes on the harder terrain, where the rules ran out and the question of what a private company owes its users had no amendment to settle it. She could hear, in her head, Andrew's rebuttal waiting for her there, and she let it wait.

At the mock court on Thursday, Ms. Pierre sat in the middle of the panel in a borrowed judge's robe that was slightly too long. When Savannah finished her concession and turned to the values argument, one of the student justices leaned forward. "So which is it? Did his rights get violated or not?" Savannah held her notes against the lectern and did not look at them. "By the website, no. The First Amendment limits the government. It doesn't by itself stop a private company from restricting speech." She paused, and the room waited. "Whether something else was violated, that's what I'd like to argue."

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: An INNER JOIN returns only rows that have a match in both tables, so customers with no orders disappear from its results entirely.
story:
The office was empty on Saturday except for the hum of a printer someone had left on, and Jonathan sat at his mother's desk with two monitors and a legal pad covered in table names. The report was due Monday morning. Her manager wanted a list of customers who had placed no orders in the last quarter, and she had volunteered Jonathan because he was "good with computers," a phrase she used to cover everything from formatting spreadsheets to, apparently, writing SQL.

He had the two tables in front of him on a sticky note his mother had written: CUSTOMERS and ORDERS. The database lived on a machine under the desk, and after an hour of guessing at passwords he had found the right one taped inside the drawer, which told him something about office security he chose not to think about.

Alistair had sent him a query at eleven that morning, pasted into a chat window with the message "this should work, lmk." It joined the customers to their orders and counted the results, and Jonathan had run it twice, thinking he'd made a typo. It returned four hundred and eleven rows, every single one with at least one order. According to the summary screen, there were five hundred and six customers in the table. Ninety-five of them had simply not appeared, and none of them were the customers with zero orders, because there were no customers with zero orders in the output at all.

He called Alistair, who was at basketball practice and whispered into the phone from the bleachers. "It's an inner join," Alistair said. "That's what the examples online used, so I copied it."

Jonathan wrote INNER JOIN on the legal pad and underlined it twice. "I think that's the problem."

"I have to go, Coach is looking." The line went dead.

Jonathan opened a new window on the second monitor and typed the same query with one word changed, LEFT JOIN, because he'd found a forum thread where someone with the username maxym_v had argued about this exact thing for two pages. The result came back in under a second: five hundred and six rows. He scrolled to the bottom and there they were, the customers with nothing in the orders column, ninety-five of them, their names sitting in the results with a blank where the order count should be. So that was it: an inner join returned only rows that had a match in both tables, which meant customers with no orders disappeared from its results entirely. They didn't show up as zero. They didn't show up at all. He sat back in his mother's chair and looked at the ceiling tile for a while.

The intercom on the desk crackled, which startled him, because he'd assumed he was alone. It was Mr. Chea from the second floor, who came in on weekends to reconcile invoices and who had so far been reticent about Jonathan's presence, offering only a nod each time they passed in the corridor. "You're the son," Mr. Chea said through the speaker. "Your mother said you'd be fixing the customer list."

"Trying to," Jonathan said into the intercom, feeling absurd talking to a building. "It's mostly done."

"Good. They wanted it for the Monday meeting." A pause. "Tell your mother the Vasquez account is not her fault, whatever anyone says in there. She shouldn't let them vilify her for it. Half that floor are sycophants and the other half are afraid of the first half."

Jonathan didn't know what to say to that, so he said, "Okay," and Mr. Chea's channel clicked off.

He spent the afternoon being careful. He ran the left join version three more times, then wrote a second query from scratch to cross-check the count, and the numbers agreed. He formatted the ninety-five names into a document, checked the spelling of the company names against the original table, and saved two copies, one to his mother's folder and one to his own email. At four o'clock he printed a draft, and the forgotten printer by the window woke up with a groan and pushed the pages out one at a time.

When he had the full stack, he read it through once. Somewhere in the middle was a customer named Ondrusek, some supplier in Brno, and at the end were three rows his query had flagged with a warning he didn't fully understand yet, something about null values in a field he hadn't selected. He circled them in pencil. His mother would be back Monday at seven, the meeting was at nine, and he could fix the three rows tomorrow, or he could leave the circles for her, or he could try again tonight and risk breaking something that currently worked. He turned the monitor off, stacked the pages on the desk, squared their edges against the blotter, and set his pencil down on top of them, point toward the three circles.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In soccer, being in an offside position is not an offence by itself; a player is penalized only when involved in active play, and there is no offside from a throw-in, goal kick or corner.
story:
Grandfather's television was older than Autumn was, and it showed the match in colors that made the green field look like pond water. The whole living room had arranged itself around that screen by four o'clock: Grandfather in his chair, the one he claimed was autochthonous to the spot, as though it had grown there like a tree; Autumn's mother on the couch with a bowl of pretzels she guarded like contraband; and on the floor, Kylan and Memphis, who had biked over because Autumn's grandfather had the only television in the neighborhood that would be showing the semi-final at all.

It was the sixty-eighth minute, the score tied at one, when the corner kick came in. The striker rose at the far post, entirely alone, entirely beyond the last defender, and headed the ball into the net with the kind of violence that made everyone in the room flinch except Grandfather, who was already on his feet.

"Offside!" he bellowed. "He was miles off! Disgraceful!"

Autumn had been half asleep against the couch cushions, but the shouting pulled her upright. The replays were already rolling. The striker had been past the last defender, that much was true, and yet the referee was pointing to the center circle, and none of the defenders were appealing, and the commentators weren't even discussing it, as though the question had never existed.

"Grandpa, it came from a corner," she said.

"I know what I saw. He was off. They've stopped calling it."

Memphis, who maintained that supporting this team at all was a kind of nihilism, an endless devotion to a thing that gave nothing back, spread his hands. "Even if he was off, they've restarted. Kickoff. It's done, old man."

"It is not done." Grandfather's voice could have carried across an actual stadium. "I have watched this sport for fifty years."

Autumn reached for her phone and then stopped herself, because she remembered something else first, something from the dusty back fields where her league played. She was eleven, maybe twelve, standing in an offside position for a full minute while the ball got recycled sideways and sideways again, and finally she jogged back onside before it ever came near her, and afterward the coach had told her something that had stuck. You could stand out there all afternoon, he'd said. Being in an offside position wasn't an offence by itself. You only got penalized when you became involved, when the ball came to you, when you touched the play.

"I don't think you're penalized just for being there," she said slowly. "Only if you're actually involved in the play."

"The ball went to his head," Grandfather said. "That is involved."

"But it was a corner. Wait." She held up a hand, working through it. The throw-in was the other thing, from a match two springs ago when Kylan had stood in an offside position directly from a throw and scored, and the ref had let it stand, and Kylan had spent the entire walk home insisting he'd known all along. She turned to him. "That goal you scored sophomore year. Off the throw-in."

"I remember it fondly," Kylan said. "It was my finest hour."

"You were offside when you took it."

"There's no offside from a throw-in," Kylan said, with the serene confidence of someone quoting scripture. "Also no offside from a goal kick. Also no offside from a corner."

"There," Autumn said, and it landed in her all at once, the way a solved thing lands. "There's no offside from a corner. That's why nobody's appealing. He could stand behind the whole team if he wanted, on a corner, and it's legal."

Grandfather looked at the screen, where the striker was now being embraced by three teammates and the crowd was singing something half inaudible. The clock in the corner showed seventy-one minutes. Nineteen minutes left, and Grandfather had money on this match, five dollars with Autumn's mother, settled at full time, and he was not a man who paid a bet he considered unjust.

"Look it up," he said. "On the telephone."

"I don't need to."

"Look it up anyway."

She looked it up. She read the laws to herself, the same ones her memory had already assembled: no offence in being in an offside position, only in being involved in active play, and no offside at all from a throw-in, a goal kick, or a corner. She turned the phone around so he could see it.

Grandfather took the phone, held it at arm's length, and read it twice. His expression went through several stages, none of which he would have described aloud. Down on the floor, Memphis was laughing into a pillow, and Kylan had begun a slow, ceremonial golf clap, which Grandfather ignored with the dignity of a man pretending the room was empty.

"Fifty years," Grandfather said at last, "and nobody ever told me that."

"That's what happens when you shout at the television instead of asking it questions," Autumn's mother said, and stole a pretzel.

The seventy-ninth minute arrived with a penalty appeal, a yellow card, and Grandfather rising out of his chair again, and Autumn settled back into the cushions beside him, shoulder against his sleeve, and decided she would wait until full time to ask him whether he still thought the goal was disgraceful or whether he was quietly, privately pleased to have learned something new about a sport he had loved badly and completely for fifty years.

"What are you smiling at?" Grandfather said, not looking away from the screen.

"Nothing, Grandpa."

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: In Agatha Christie's 1926 novel The Murder of Roger Ackroyd, the narrator, Dr Sheppard, turns out to be the murderer.
story:
The reading nook was really just the window seat in Mason's room, widened by two cushions and a lamp his mother had rescued from the garage, but since September he had claimed it as territory. He sat there on a Thursday night in March with The Murder of Roger Ackroyd open on his knees, a pencil behind his ear, and his phone buzzing every few minutes against the sill.

The buzzing was Chanelle, who was stuck on the same book. "I don't get what Mr. Oyelaran wants from us," she'd said at school, dropping into the seat beside him in the cafeteria, drumming her fingers on his copy. "It's a mystery. Someone did it. The detective finds out. What's to analyse?" Simeon, across the table, hadn't looked up from his economics notes. "Analyse this instead," he'd said. "Explain stagflation to me before Friday, because right now my grade depends on it and I understand nothing." He'd said the word the way people say a diagnosis.

Mason hadn't answered Chanelle then. He'd said something vague about point of view, and she'd rolled her eyes, and now, forty pages from the end, he understood that his vagueness had been a kind of lie. Because he'd just read the chapter where everything turned over, and the floor of the book had dropped out from under him.

He picked up the phone. "It's the narrator," he said when Chanelle answered. "The whole time."

"The narrator of what?"

"The book. The Murder of Roger Ackroyd. The narrator, Dr Sheppard, turns out to be the murderer."

There was a silence long enough that he could hear her television in the background. "You're joking."

"Why would I joke about this at eleven at night?"

"Because he's the one telling us everything. He's the one who found the body. He was, like, sympathetic." Her voice climbed. "He makes tea for the detective. He makes tea for the detective, Mason."

That was the thing, he thought, or began to think, pulling his knees up. The tea was the crime, or part of it. He turned back to the first chapter, hunting, and there it was, or something like it: the narrator describing his own evening with a flatness that read as calm, a man setting down what he did and omitting what mattered. Mason underlined a sentence and then, feeling something almost atavistic in it, the old animal wariness of realizing you have been watched by something watching you back, underlined it twice.

"He hid it in plain sight," he told Chanelle. "I'm rereading the opening chapters. He never exactly lies, he just, stops."

"Stops where?"

"Where it counts. He narrates what he did after the murder like it's ordinary, because it was ordinary, for him." Mason was talking faster now, pencil moving. "So the question isn't who did it, it's why we believed him. The point of view, Chanelle. That's what shapes our trust. He had us predicate the whole book on his honesty, and the book was built on that."

"Say the last part again slower, I'm writing this down."

"I'm not doing your essay for you."

"You're doing it for you, and I'm eavesdropping. It's different."

He laughed, and it caught in his throat a little, because there was a loss in it too. He had liked Dr Sheppard. He had liked the dry voice, the village routines, the way the man described his sister's chatter with weary affection, and all of that affection was still real on the page, still well made, and still the instrument of the deception. It was like discovering a friend kept a ledger of your weaknesses. He couldn't decide whether the book was crueler for it or better.

The next afternoon Mr. Oyelaran collected their reading journals with the unhurried air of a man who knew most of them had written the same discovery in different handwritings. He paused at Mason's desk. "You found him, then."

"I found him. I still don't know if I forgive him."

"That's not a small reaction." Mr. Oyelaran tapped the journal once and moved on, and Mason watched him go, dissatisfied, wanting a verdict, wanting someone to tell him what he was allowed to feel about a fictional man who had lied to him for two hundred pages.

That evening Simeon sprawled on the window seat while Mason tried to explain the trick a second time, for the pleasure of it. "So the guy telling you the story is the guy who did it," Simeon said, "and you only find out because you keep reading."

"Because I kept reading. Chanelle figured it out the same night, over the phone."

"And nothing else about the story changes?"

"Everything about it changes. But the words are all the same words."
