Mason looked down at the underlined sentence, the one he'd marked twice, which had seemed like a confession when he found it and which now, on the tenth reading, could be an innocent man describing his evening. The lamp hummed. Outside, a car door slammed somewhere down the street.

"You still trust any of it?" Simeon asked.

Mason closed the book on his pencil and looked at the cover, at the small printed figure on it, standing in a garden, waiting.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: In translation, the ribosome moves along the messenger RNA and joins amino acids together with peptide bonds to build a protein chain.
story:
The retake was scheduled for Friday, which gave Henry four days to understand something he had spent three weeks failing to understand. He sat at the back lab bench during lunch with the textbook open to a diagram he had copied twice already, once neatly and once in desperation, and neither version had helped. Alden dropped his bag beside him and looked over his shoulder.

"You failed that one too?" Alden asked. "The transcription thing?"

"I got the DNA part," Henry said. "Mostly. It's the rest of it. Every time I read it, it's like the words slide off."

Alden pulled out a sandwich and did not offer to share it, which was usual. "Lea-Rose got the highest mark in the class. She said it's actually easy once you see it. Which is an insulting thing to say, but she might be right."

Lea-Rose was already in the lab, two benches up, working on her own retake prep for a different class entirely, because she was the sort of person who did extra studying for classes she was already passing. Henry walked over with the diagram and set it in front of her, and she looked at it the way she looked at badly parked bicycles, with mild dismay but a willingness to fix things.

"Okay," she said. "Forget the diagram. Forget the word transcription for a second. You know how to thread beads?"

"What?"

"Beads. On a string. Say you have a pattern on paper and you're threading beads to match it. What do you do?"

"You look at the pattern, you pick the bead, you put it on the string. Then the next one."

"Right, and you keep going down the pattern, one bead at a time, and each bead sits next to the one before it. Now say the pattern is the messenger RNA. And the beads are amino acids." She tapped the diagram. "The thing doing the threading, the thing that moves along the messenger RNA reading the pattern, that's the ribosome. And it doesn't just set the beads next to each other. It joins them. The bonds between the amino acids are called peptide bonds. So the whole string of them is a protein."

Henry stared at the diagram and something rearranged itself, not with a flash, more like a door that had been stuck finally swinging on its hinge. "So the protein isn't built somewhere else and then matched up. It's built as the ribosome goes."

"Along the messenger RNA, yes. Reading and threading at the same time. That's the whole miracle of it, honestly. It's slow and stupid and it works."

Henry carried the diagram back to his bench, and Alden raised his eyebrows. "Miracle?" Alden said, having apparently heard. "It's a chemistry exam, not a cathedral."

"It's both, kind of." Henry said this and then heard how it sounded, and Alden laughed at him, but Henry kept the thought anyway. He had spent weeks treating the material as a list of terms to be memorized, an approach that had exonerated him from actually understanding anything, since memorizing felt like work and produced a page of honest-looking notes. His grasp of it had stayed inchoate, a fog of vocabulary with nothing holding it together. What Lea-Rose had done in two minutes was give him the string. The pattern, the beads, the hand moving down the line. He copied the diagram a third time, and this time he drew the ribosome as a little circle with a hand, which was not scientific but which he could see.

Mr. Castillo came around the lab during the last part of lunch, collecting his beakers from the demonstrations, and paused at Henry's bench. He looked at the drawing with the hand for a long moment.

"That's not how it's drawn in the textbook," he said.

"I know. It's how I remember it."

Mr. Castillo set down the beakers. "The exam will want the real terms. Ribosome, messenger RNA, peptide bonds, amino acids."

"I know all of those now," Henry said. "Yesterday I knew them and didn't know anything. Today I know them and I know what they're doing." He heard the boldness of it and waited to be told he was wrong, because Mr. Castillo had a reputation, not entirely fair, as a bit of an autocrat about right answers and wrong ones.

Mr. Castillo picked up the drawing and studied it. "Draw it both ways tonight," he said finally. "Your way and the textbook's way, side by side. If you can move between them, you understand it. If you can only do your way, you've just invented a second thing to memorize." He put the paper down and carried his beakers to the front, and Henry sat there feeling both corrected and, somehow, encouraged.

Friday morning he opened the exam and found the question, and the diagram was there, and he could see the little hand moving in his mind, reading the pattern, joining each bead to the last with its peptide bond, building the chain as it traveled. He wrote quickly, then stopped, then wrote again, because there was one part near the end he was still not sure of, the part where the string is finished, and he left a small mark beside it, a question to himself, and moved on. When he handed the paper in, Lea-Rose was already at the door.

"Beads?" she asked.

"Beads," Henry said. "And one thing I still don't know."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At a Passover Seder the youngest child present customarily asks the Four Questions from the Haggadah, beginning with 'Why is this night different from all other nights?'
story:
Mathis arrived at his aunt's house with his collar already wilting, because the March heat had metastasized from a mild afternoon into something tropical, and the driveway was full of cars he half recognized. Inside, the folding tables had been arranged into one long spine down the living room, and his grandmother was directing traffic with a stack of Haggadot like a general with battle plans. Somewhere near the bookshelf, his nine-year-old cousin Courtney was mouthing words to herself with the grim concentration of a student about to defend a thesis.

"Why is this night different," Courtney whispered, "from all other nights?" Then she stopped, frowned, and started over.

"Ballpark's fine," Mathis said, dropping onto the arm of the couch beside her. "Nobody's grading you."

"Aunt Rachel is grading me," Courtney said. "She has a face."

She did have a face. It was the face of a woman who believed that rituals, like soufflés, collapsed at the slightest wobble. Mathis remembered wearing that face himself at nine, holding the little book with damp hands while the whole table turned toward him like a jury. He had gotten through it, barely, and afterward his grandfather had squeezed his shoulder and said nothing, which in that family was a standing ovation.

The problem revealed itself early, during the first glass of grape juice. Courtney slid next to Mathis on the bench and said, very quietly, "I can't do the order. There are four of them and they all start the same and I get lost."

"You're the youngest at the table," Mathis said. "That's the whole job. The youngest kid asks the Four Questions, it starts the Seder. Everyone else just has to eat slowly and pretend they're patient."

"Four," Courtney repeated, like the number itself was a small insult. She pulled the Haggadah onto her lap and turned it sideways, as though the questions might read differently at an angle.

At the far end of the table, Mr. Karimi from next door, who came every year because he said his own grandmother in Tehran had told the Exodus story better than anyone, was already debating the proper amount of horseradish with an uncle. Mathis liked Mr. Karimi, who treated every tradition as both sacred and slightly ridiculous, which struck Mathis as the only sane position. When Courtney wasn't looking, Mathis ducked into the hallway and called Caden, who had a younger sister and therefore, in Mathis's view, proprietary knowledge of small frightened children.

"Trick them into teaching you," Caden said over the noise of his own family's dinner. "Ask her to explain it to her stuffed animal. My sister rehearses on a penguin. The penguin has never once asked a clarifying question."

This was the kind of advice that sounded like a confounder, a variable that would only muddy things further, but it was also, annoyingly, the only advice on offer. Mathis went back to the living room, found Courtney's canvas bag, and extracted a one-eared rabbit with the sincerity of a surgeon retrieving an organ. He set it on her lap.

"Rabbit doesn't know the Seder at all," Mathis said. "Total beginner. He's never even had charoset. You're going to have to take him through it, from the top, and he's going to need it slow."

Courtney looked at the rabbit. Courtney looked at Mathis. There was a pause during which the entire evening seemed to balance on a dime. "He'd be nervous," she decided. "If everyone was staring at him."

"Terribly nervous," Mathis agreed. "Shaking, probably. Rabbits shake."

So while the candles were lit and the adults argued about whether to skip a page, Courtney bent over the rabbit's one ear and walked it through all four, from the dipping of vegetables to the reclining, stumbling twice and correcting herself without being asked, and by the third pass she had stopped whispering. When the moment came and the room quieted and every face turned toward the youngest person at the table, Courtney sat up straight, glanced once at the rabbit peeking out of her bag, and asked why this night was different from all other nights, clear enough to reach the kitchen.

Later, elbow-deep in dishes, Mathis caught his aunt's eye over the suds. She raised the sponge toward the doorway, where Courtney was asleep against the rabbit on the good chair.

"Four for four," his aunt said. "You coached her."

"The rabbit coached her," Mathis said. "I just did logistics."

Mr. Karimi appeared beside the sink with a towel, drying plates with the calm efficiency of a man who had done this in three countries. "In my grandmother's house," he said, "the youngest always asked the questions, and the smartest one in the room always pretended not to know the answers. You have a head start on pretending. Keep practicing."

Mathis handed him the next plate and, down the hall, someone dropped a piece of matzah, and the whole table groaned as one.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: In many tax systems, a deduction lowers the income that tax is calculated on, while a tax credit subtracts directly from the tax owed, so a credit is usually worth more than an equal deduction.
story:
The queue at the bank moved in small, reluctant shuffles, and Isla held her folder of papers against her chest like a shield that was failing. Inside were her first tax return, her last three paycheques from the grocery store, and a receipt from the campus bookstore that had startled her in September, when a textbook she had priced at ninety dollars had cost her a hundred and change at the till. She had stood there while the cashier bagged it, staring at the line marked HST, understanding only that some portion of her money was leaving her twice, once visibly and once not.

She reached the counter and told the teller she needed to deposit her paycheque and then, if possible, sit with someone about her return. The teller pointed to a desk near the window, where a man in a grey suit was already gesturing at a computer screen. Beside the desk, in the waiting chairs, sat Kaitlin from her Grade Twelve economics class, filling out a form on her knee.

"Isla. Small world," Kaitlin said, not looking up. "I'm here because my mother refuses to believe the government owes her money. I intend to prove it with documents." She tapped her folder. "Documents are how you win against a parent. What's your emergency?"

"Apparently I owe them. Or I don't. The software says one thing and my dad says another and I don't know which of them to trust." Isla sat down beside her. "My dad's position is that I shouldn't file at all because I barely made anything. My position is that I don't want to be circumspect about it forever and then get audited at thirty."

Kaitlin laughed. "That's not what circumspect means, exactly, but I take your point." She set down her pen. "Show me."

Isla opened the folder and spread the papers between them on the little table. The paycheque was the first thing, its stub dense with lines: gross pay, then a column of deductions, Canada Pension Plan, Employment Insurance, income tax, each one taking its small agreed-upon share until the net pay at the bottom looked thin and honest. She had worked forty-one hours over two weeks and held something like thirty-two of them.

"They take it before you even see it," Kaitlin said. "That part I knew. The sales tax is the other direction. You see it, and you pay it anyway." She held up the bookstore receipt, which Isla hadn't realized she'd brought. "You kept this?"

"It was in the folder. I keep everything. It's a condition." Isla took it back and smoothed it flat. Ninety dollars for the book, then tax, then a total that had made her recalculate her food budget for October. She had eaten a lot of rice that month, and had told herself it was a choice, a kind of experiment, which it partly was.

The man in the grey suit left his desk, and Ms. Park, who Isla realized she recognized from the branch near her old school, waved them over. Behind the desk, Kaitlin slid her own form forward first, because Kaitlin always went first. While Ms. Park reviewed it, Kaitlin explained her mother's situation with the air of a lawyer opening a case, and Isla watched the numbers on the screen rearrange themselves, deductions and credits sorted into separate columns, as though the software were a customs officer sorting incoming travellers.

Then it was Isla's turn. Ms. Park asked about tuition, and Isla pulled out the form from the university, and there it was, the thing that had confused her for two weeks: an amount she could claim, and two different places she could claim it, and no intuition at all about which was better. She had assumed the bigger number was the better number. She typed one way, then the other, watching the amount owing at the bottom of the screen.

"Wait," she said. Both of them looked at her. "The deduction lowers the income they calculate the tax on. The credit subtracts from the tax I owe. So the credit comes off the end, after everything." She moved the claim from one box to the other, and the amount she owed shrank, more than it had before, though the claimed number was the same number.

"That's why Dad's wrong," Isla said. "I'm getting money back. Some." She recalibrated her expectations downward immediately, because there would be a bus pass and a winter coat and the second textbook she'd been putting off, but it was real, it was hers, it had already belonged to her all year without her knowing.

Ms. Park printed a confirmation page, and Kaitlin, triumphant over her own refund, insisted they walk to the bakery two doors down to celebrate with something Isla could now technically afford. On the way, Kaitlin said her mother would deny the refund was real until it cleared, and probably after. Isla thought of her dad at the kitchen table saying nobody taxes a kid, and of the antigen of that idea in her family, something the body had always accepted, and knew she would show him the paper anyway, and that whether he changed his mind was his business, not hers.

At the counter Isla counted out the coins for a loaf of bread still warm through the paper bag, and decided she would buy the second textbook on Monday, full price, tax and all.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: US inflation peaked at 14.8 percent in March 1980 and fell below 3 percent by 1983, after the Federal Reserve's sharp interest rate increases.
story:
Nathaniel had agreed to meet Allyson at the farmers' market because his mother had taken over the kitchen for a canning project and because Allyson had texted that the market had "tables, which are basically desks." She was already there when he arrived, installed between a crate of Roma tomatoes and a woman selling soap shaped like owls, with the inflation graph from their econ packet flattened under a mason jar of honey she hadn't paid for yet.

"I don't get 1980," Allyson said, before he'd even sat down. She tapped the line on the graph that climbed like a staircase and then fell off a cliff. "Everything before this makes sense. Prices go up, people get mad, the graph goes up. Then this. It just drops. What happened, everyone got tired?"

"Something happened," Nathaniel said. He had read the packet twice on the bus, and the paragraph about the early eighties had a way of rearranging itself in his memory every time he approached it, an inchoate sense that the Federal Reserve had done something drastic, the specifics dissolving whenever he tried to hold them still.

"Great. I'll write that on the quiz. 'Something happened.'"

Down the row, a vendor was arguing with someone about whether the peach season had been ruined by rain or merely humbled by it, and the soap woman was explaining to a customer that the owls were lavender, not "perfumey." Nathaniel pulled out his phone and found the number again, the one that had surprised him the first time and surprised him again now: inflation had peaked at 14.8 percent in March of 1980. Fourteen point eight. His mother's first car loan had been at eleven, and she still talked about it the way people talked about wars.

"It was almost fifteen percent," he said. "In March 1980. That's the peak, right there, that's the top stair."

Allyson frowned at the graph. "Fifteen percent of what?"

"Of everything. Of prices, going up, per year. So by 1983, look, it's under three percent. That's the drop. That's what we have to explain." He said it with more confidence than he had, because the numbers at least were solid, and solidity felt like a resource he should spend while he had it.

"What did the Fed do, lower prices by hand?" She picked up the honey jar and put it down again, leaving a ring on the graph like a small moon.

"Raised interest rates." He said it and then waited, the way you wait after setting down a heavy box, to see whether it held. Allyson's face suggested it did not hold. "Rates went up sharply. That's in the packet. And then inflation came down, from that peak, all the way to under three percent, by 1983."

"That's backwards. If something costs too much, you make it cheaper to borrow?"

"There was a fight about it," Nathaniel said. "That's the part I keep losing. There's a way of thinking where you look at that drop and think, somebody decided something was going to be true and then made it true, and everybody had to live inside that decision. And there's another way where you think, no, that's just what the numbers did, and the person in charge happened to be standing there." He had been circling between those two all week, unable to commit, and hearing himself say it out loud didn't settle anything so much as delimit the shape of what he didn't know. "I can't tell which one I'm supposed to believe. I can't even tell if they're different."

"That's very comforting," Allyson said. "I'm going to write 'Nathaniel can't tell' in the margin."

Ms. Cruz, who taught junior English and kept a stall at the market on Saturdays, mostly jams, had drifted over somewhere during the interest rates part and was now standing there with a crate of Damson plum preserves, not pretending she hadn't been listening. "My father refinanced his shop three times that year," she said. "Nineteen eighty-one. He said the bank was either saving the country or killing him, and he never found out which."

"That's exactly the problem," Nathaniel said. "He's both of them. The graph is the whole country and it's also one guy with a shop."

"He kept the shop," Ms. Cruz said. "He also kept a speech about banks that lasted until he died. Solvency, he called it. His whole pride in himself was that word." She shifted the crate to her other hip. "I have no idea what any of it means, I teach freshman composition. I just like eavesdropping on people who study money. You all sound like priests."

She carried her plums off toward her stall. Allyson looked at the graph, at the little honey moon, at the drop.

"So for the write-up," she said, "I put the numbers, the peak and then under three by '83, and that the Fed raised rates sharply. And then what?"

"Then you say the drop happened after the raises," Nathaniel said. "You don't say it was because of them. You say you don't know."

"The quiz is going to love that."

"The quiz wants a priest," he said. "We're giving it a person."

Allyson paid for the honey, finally, and the soap woman watched her count out the bills with the protective attention of someone whose livelihood was shaped like owls. Behind them Ms. Cruz was telling a customer that the Damson was the superior plum, and the customer was saying she'd take four, and neither of them looked at the sky, which had gone the flat gray that meant the market would pack up early.

"Under three percent," Allyson said, zipping her bag. "By 1983. Fine. If I fail, I'm telling Ms. Cruz it was your graph."

"It was my graph," Nathaniel said, and folded it, honey ring and all, into his pocket.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Properly tempered chocolate shrinks slightly as it sets, which helps it release cleanly from a mould.
story:
I was not making chocolates for Curtis's party specifically, whatever Tristan says. I was making chocolates because I wanted to learn something precise, and precision was the one thing I was short of that spring. My marks had gone soft in every subject except chemistry, and even chemistry felt like guessing in a lab coat. So on a Saturday in March, with my mother out and the kitchen to myself, I bought two bars of dark chocolate and a silicone mould shaped like little domes, and I told myself this was practice for a kind of person I intended to become.

I did not need Curtis's approval. I want that on the record. But Curtis was an aesthete of the worst kind, the kind who notices your shoes and says nothing, and at lunch he had looked at the photo of a chocolatier's glossy bonbons on my phone and said, "You'd never get that at home." Tristan heard it too. Tristan hears everything and metabolizes it into material, which is either his charm or his flaw, and he showed up at my door that Saturday with a thermometer he'd borrowed from the chemistry lab and a look of pure, insouciant confidence, as if he already knew how this would go.

"Tempering," he announced, reading off his phone. "You melt it, cool it, warm it again. Something about crystals." He waved the sentence away like smoke. "How hard can it be?"

It turned out that the melting was the easy part. The chocolate went liquid and gorgeous in the bowl over the simmering pot, and I stirred it with the patience of a monk, and we spooned it into the domes and tapped out the bubbles and put the mould in the fridge like two people who believed the fridge was a finishing school. An hour later the chocolates had set. They were dull, the surface cloudy as a breath on a window, and when I turned the mould over and flexed it, nothing came out. I flexed harder. One dome tore in half and stayed in its cavity like something that had decided to live there.

"It's stuck," Tristan said, unnecessarily.

"They're stuck," I said. "And it's fine. Silicone is supposed to be nonstick." I pried the second one out with a knife and it came up scarred, a pale gouge across its back. I put the knife down very carefully, because the alternative was throwing it, and I said the thing I had been refusing to think. "Maybe it never set right. Maybe it was never actually in temper."

Tristan looked at his phone again. "Says here properly tempered chocolate shrinks slightly as it sets. That's why it comes out of the mould clean. It pulls away from the sides." He said it in the tone of a person reporting a bus schedule, which somehow made it worse and better at the same time. I stood there with my ruined chocolates lined up on a plate, matte and stubborn and half of them mangled, and understood that I hadn't failed at releasing them. I had failed much earlier, at a stage where nothing visible goes wrong.

So we started again, and this time I paid attention like it was the only attention I had. Melted, then off the heat, then chopped chocolate stirred in until the bowl lost its shine and began to thicken, then back over the warmth for seconds only, watching the thermometer like it owed me money. Tristan kept his hands behind his back, which was wise of him. I poured, tapped, chilled. Then came the part I hadn't known to prepare for, the quiet of it. The chocolates came out with a snap when I flexed the mould, all twelve of them at once, tumbling onto the plate glossy as lacquer, each one just slightly smaller than its cavity had been. I heard the shrinkage more than saw it, that soft collective click of chocolate letting go.

Here is where I have to be honest, because Tristan will tell it differently at school anyway. I ate two of them standing up, and then I packed eight into a box for Curtis's party, and only as I was tying the ribbon did I admit that I had known Curtis's name in my head the whole time, that every glossy dome was a small argument aimed at a person who hadn't asked for one. The gain and the loss sat on the same plate. I had learned the thing, really learned it, and I had learned it partly for someone who might not notice, and there was no separating those two facts no matter how I turned them over, the way I had turned over the mould.

At the party Curtis took one chocolate, bit it, and said, "Where did you buy these?" Tristan opened his mouth to correct him. I picked up another dome myself, snapped it in half, and looked at the clean break.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Raising the temperature speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions, but it speeds up the endothermic direction more, which is why the equilibrium shifts that way.
story:
The retake was at eight the next morning, and Taylor had until then to understand why her first answer had been wrong. The quiz question had asked what happens to a reaction at equilibrium when you raise the temperature, and she had written that everything speeds up equally, so nothing changes. Ms. Kobayashi had circled it in red and written one word in the margin: rethink. No explanation, no partial credit. Taylor sat at the kitchen table with her notes, two strips of cobalt chloride paper from the lab kit she had signed out, a mug of water, and her phone propped against the sugar jar with Jasmin on video call.

"I still think your first answer makes sense," Jasmin said. "Heat is energy. Energy makes molecules move faster. Both directions should go faster."

"That's what I said. And it was wrong."

"Then the whole thing is wrong," Jasmin said, and bit into an apple.

Taylor had the handout from the failed quiz in front of her. At the top, Ms. Kobayashi had printed a statement about Le Chatelier's principle, and below it, three sentences about rate constants that Taylor had skipped the first time because they looked like math. She read them now. Both the forward and the reverse reaction have their own rates, the handout said, and temperature changes each of them.

"Okay," Taylor said slowly. "So it doesn't speed them up the same."

"Why wouldn't it?"

"I don't know yet. Give me a second."

She microwaved the mug until steam came off it, then dipped one cobalt strip. The paper was pink at room temperature; in the hot water it turned blue within a count of about four. She wrote that down. Then she ran the tap until the water ran cold, filled a glass, and dipped a second strip. The same pink paper went blue in the cold water too, eventually, but it took much longer, long enough that she counted past twenty and Jasmin started laughing at her on the screen.

"You're timing paper," Jasmin said.

"I'm collecting data. It turned blue both times. Hot was faster. Four versus twenty-something." She set the hot strip on the counter and the cold one beside it and stared at them. "So the forward reaction, the one that goes to blue, happens in both directions. That means there's a reverse one too, blue back to pink."

"You can't see that."

"I can if I change the temperature of the strip itself." She put the blue strip from the cold glass into the mug of hot water and waited. It stayed blue. She put the other blue strip against the ice tray, pressing it flat with her palm, and after a while the edges began to flush pink, creeping inward while the center held. She took a photo of it, half and half, like a bruise.

"Fine, it goes backward," Jasmin said. "Slowly. So what?"

Taylor pulled the handout closer. The strip against the ice was still changing, the pink winning ground. Both things were happening at once, she thought, forward and reverse, on the same piece of paper, and the question wasn't which one ran but which one the temperature favored. She ran her finger down the handout until she found the sentence she had skipped twice: the two directions differ in whether they take in heat or give it off. "That's it," she said. "One direction is endothermic. It takes heat in like a reactant."

"You just like saying that word."

"Raising the temperature speeds up both of them," Taylor said, mostly to herself, "but it speeds up the endothermic direction more. So the whole equilibrium shifts that way. That's why the hot strip went blue fast and the cold strip went pink." She said it once more, quietly, and it held together the way a knot holds when you pull both ends.

Jasmin was unconvinced in the way she was unconvinced about most things, pleasantly, without stakes. "So on the quiz, you write that?"

"I write that."

The phone buzzed with a text before Jasmin could argue. It was from Ms. Kobayashi, sent to the whole class: the retake was moved to Thursday because of a faculty meeting, and students should use the extra time to interpolate between the examples in chapter twelve, since the test questions would fall between them, not on them. Taylor read it aloud. Jasmin said something about fate, some platitude about things working out, and Taylor nodded while not listening, because she had already picked up the half-pink strip and was carrying it toward the mug.

She had learned the thing one day early, from a piece of paper and a mug of water, with no test in the morning to make it matter. She dipped the strip in the hot water and watched the pink go quiescent, then retreat, then vanish, blue spreading from the edges inward exactly as the pink had spread on the ice, and she held it there under the surface until the last of it turned.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: In The Old Regime and the Revolution, published in 1856, Alexis de Tocqueville argued the Revolution continued the centralization of power already begun under the French monarchy.
story:
The city archive smelled of dust that had been organized, which Jessica found oddly comforting. She had claimed a table near the microfilm readers, where the lamp buzzed at a pitch only she seemed to hear, and spread out her notes like evidence at a trial no one was attending. Her essay was due in three weeks. The assignment, Mr. Sánchez had announced with what she suspected was private amusement, was not about the French Revolution at all. It was about what people had said about the French Revolution since 1800, which meant Jessica had to care about the historians almost as much as the history.

Her problem, so far, was that every historian disagreed with every other historian and all of them wrote as though disagreement were a moral failing. She had a stack of photocopies, a headache, and one sentence that she liked: interpretations of the Revolution, she had written, reveal more about the century in which they were written than about 1789. Then she had crossed it out because it sounded cleverer than it was certain.

Imogen arrived twenty minutes late, carrying a coffee the size of a fire extinguisher. "You realize people our age are at the river right now," she said, dropping into the chair across from Jessica.

"People our age will fail Mr. Sánchez's class."

"He likes you. He let you have the archive pass."

"He let anyone with a permission slip have the archive pass. Nobody else wanted one." Jessica slid a photocopy across the table. It was from a survey of nineteenth-century French historiography, a chapter she had requested more out of desperation than design. "Read the part I underlined. Twice, if you can stand it."

Imogen read, moving her lips slightly in a way that would have annoyed Jessica if she had not been doing the same thing an hour earlier. "Tocqueville," Imogen said. "In The Old Regime and the Revolution, published in 1856, he argued the Revolution continued the centralization of power already begun under the French monarchy." She looked up. "Continued it. Not started it."

"That's the part that's bothering me."

"Bothering you how?"

Jessica pulled her notebook toward her and drew two arrows that met in the middle. On the left she wrote monarchy, on the right Revolution. "Everything I've read treats the Revolution as a rupture. Something new under the sun. And then this man, thirty years after the Paris archive burned, sits down and says the Revolution didn't break with the monarchy's way of running things, it kept going with it. The kings had already been gathering power toward the center. The Revolutionaries just, what, inherited the machinery?" She stopped, aware she was guessing. "I don't actually know what he meant by that. I only know that he said it, and that everyone after him had to deal with it."

"You could ask Mr. Sánchez."

"He'd give me a reading list. I'd be in the same morass with more footnotes."

Randy turned up at noon, ostensibly to study for a chemistry test, actually because the archive was air conditioned and he had heard the vending machine gave two drinks for one. He leaned over Jessica's notes with the caution of a man approaching a dog he didn't trust. "So the Revolution was fake?" he said.

"Nobody said fake."

"You just said it copied the monarchy."

"Continued," Imogen said, with the precision of someone who had read the sentence twice. "It continued the centralization already begun under the monarchy. That's what he argued in the book. It came out in 1856."

Randy considered this while extracting his second drink from the machine. "So France before 1789 and France after 1789, same thing, different flags."

"That is," Jessica said, "the incisive summary I will not be putting in my essay." But later, alone again while Imogen and Randy argued about electrolytes, she wrote it in the margin anyway, because it was shorter than her version and she wanted to look at it.

What she looked at, through the afternoon, was the stack of interpretations around it. The radicals who needed the Revolution to be a birth. The conservatives who needed it to be a crime. Tocqueville, arriving in the middle, saying something that fit neither team: that the old regime and the new one were connected, that the break was not as complete as either side wanted. She had spent two weeks trying to decide which historian was right. It occurred to her now, under the buzzing lamp, that a better question was what each of them needed the Revolution to be, and what Tocqueville's answer cost him with both camps.

She did not resolve it, exactly. In her draft that evening she wrote that she found Tocqueville's argument the most persuasive because it refused the comfort of a clean beginning, and then, honestly, she wrote that she was not yet sure whether she found it persuasive on its evidence or merely attractive in its contrariness, a distinction she suspected Mr. Sánchez would make her defend. She beseeched the ceiling of her bedroom for a verdict and received the usual silence.

At school the next morning she handed Mr. Sánchez the draft without ceremony. He read the first page standing in the doorway, which she took as a bad sign, and then the second, which she took as a good one.

"Most students pick a side by Friday," he said.

"I can pick a side. I just don't know yet if I'd be picking it for the right reasons."

Mr. Sánchez folded the pages lengthwise, twice, and tucked them into his folder. "Underline that sentence and keep it in the essay," he said, and walked toward the staff room.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Regular aerobic exercise, such as brisk walking or cycling on most days, lowers blood pressure in many people, including those who already have hypertension.
story:
Emilie set the borrowed cuff on the kitchen table between the salt cellar and her mother's cold tea, and read the little digital display one more time, as though the numbers might have softened while she looked away. One hundred fifty-eight over ninety-six. Her handout from the pharmacy training program, due to be demonstrated tomorrow morning at nine, said that a reading that high, taken twice, calmly, was not a number to shrug off. Her mother stood at the stove pretending to be absorbed in the rice, which did not need stirring.

"Sit down again," Emilie said. "Arm at heart level. Feet flat. Don't talk."

"I wasn't talking."

"You were about to."

Her mother sat, and Emilie wrapped the cuff the way she had practiced on Edmond's arm until he complained his fingers were going numb. The machine whirred, squeezed, and gave them one hundred fifty-five over ninety-four, close enough to the first reading that Emilie stopped hoping it was a fluke. Ms. Korhonen, who ran the Saturday sessions at the pharmacy, had warned them about this exact moment, when the practice person turns out to be someone you love. "The cuff doesn't care whose arm it's on," she had said, which at the time Emilie had found funny and now found almost malevolent, the way a machine can sit there stating a plain, unwelcome truth.

"It's high," Emilie said, before her mother could forestall her with some story about the weather or the tea. "Both numbers."

"I felt fine all week."

"That's the thing. That's why it's called hypertension, the high part. You don't feel it."

Her mother looked at her hands, then at the rice pot, and Emilie recognized the look, the one that meant she was deciding whether to treat this as a daughter's alarm or as information. Emilie wanted it to be information. She dug through her folder for the sheet she had annotated after the last session, the one Edmond had quizzed her on over the phone until nearly midnight. At the bottom, in her own handwriting, was the part she had underlined twice, because Ms. Korhonen had repeated it and because it was the part that gave her something to do instead of something to fear.

"Regular aerobic exercise," she read aloud. "Brisk walking, or cycling, most days. It lowers blood pressure in a lot of people. Even people who already have hypertension. It's not just prevention."

"What does aerobic mean, exactly?"

"Moving steady enough that you'd be breathing hard but could still talk. Like when you walk fast on purpose."

Her mother was quiet for a moment. "Your father used to bike to the depot before his knee."

"I know."

"I'm not joining a gym, Emilie."

"You don't have to. That's the point. It's walking."

She had texted Pedro while the machine ran the second time, because Pedro's whole family walked after dinner, every night, in every season, and she had wanted to know whether it was a chore or a habit. His reply had come as she was filling the kettle: "Honestly it's the best part of the day. My mom says the walking is when we actually talk. Start with thirty minutes and don't be heroic about it, my tia tried to sprint and quit in a week." She read it to her mother, who almost smiled at "don't be heroic."

Then Emilie turned her notebook sideways and drew four columns. Monday, Wednesday, Friday, Sunday, because "most days" meant most days, not Saturdays whenever it was convenient, and she knew from every abandoned resolution in the house how convenient could stretch. At the top she wrote "after dinner, before dishes," and beside Monday she wrote "the river path, the flat part." Her mother picked up the pen and added, in her small careful hand, "rain check is still a walk, umbrella." Under Saturday Emilie left the space blank, honest about its blankness, and wrote a question mark instead. Six days was most days; she was not certain whether seven would be better, or just harder to keep, and she did not pretend to be.

"I'll do the reading before we leave," Emilie said. "Every time. That way we can see it, not just feel it."

"And if it doesn't move?"

"Then we go to Dr. Anand with the numbers. But it moves for a lot of people. I want to find out if you're one of them."

Her mother looked at the schedule for a long moment, then at the cooling rice, then she got up, went to the hall, and came back wearing her walking shoes, which had been sitting by the door since spring in the way of things you mean to use. It was still light out. The river path was twenty minutes away, the flat part a little farther, and tomorrow at nine Emilie would stand in front of Ms. Korhonen with her cuff and her two readings and her half-empty Saturday, and say what she knew and what she didn't.

"Get your jacket," her mother said, holding the door open.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Biotech billionaire Patrick Soon-Shiong bought the Los Angeles Times in 2018 for $500 million, plus the assumption of pension obligations.
story:
The media studies classroom smelled of dry-erase marker and the radiator's burnt dust, and Juliette had taped two front pages to the whiteboard side by side before anyone else arrived. Both covered the same water crisis story, and both used the word "breakthrough," but one led with the state audit and the other led with the company's press release. She wanted to know why.

Mr. Khoury closed the door behind the last stragglers and looked at the pages for a long moment without commenting, which Juliette had learned was his way of approving an ambush. She had planned it that way. Her problem was simpler than the assignment and more personal: her mother had taken a buyout from the paper she'd worked at for nineteen years, and at dinner last night the family had argued about whether it mattered who owned the thing.

"Okay," Jessa said, dropping into the seat beside her and unwrapping a granola bar at eight in the morning like it was lunch. "You're doing the pages thing. Are we supposed to figure out which one's lying?"

"That's the wrong question," Michelle said from the row behind them, ebullient the way she always was before first period ran her down. "Neither one's lying. That's the scary part."

Jessa rolled her eyes, but she copied the headline down anyway.

Juliette had gone home last night and read until midnight, past the family argument, past her father's claim that rich owners were vultures and her mother's quieter claim that without one there wouldn't be a paper at all. What she found sat in her notebook now in her own handwriting: Patrick Soon-Shiong, a biotech billionaire, bought the Los Angeles Times in 2018 for 500 million dollars, plus the assumption of pension obligations. She liked the phrase "assumption of pension obligations" because it sounded like a person quietly picking up something heavy that someone else had dropped. She had repeated it to her father at the sink and he had gone silent, which for him was a concession.

When Mr. Khoury opened the floor, she stood up. "So a biotech billionaire bought the LA Times in 2018," she said. "Five hundred million, plus he assumed the pension obligations." She heard the sentence land awkwardly in the room, too factual, like a citation read aloud, and pushed past it. "And I keep going back and forth. He spent all that money, and maybe that saves the reporting. Or maybe the things he cares about are the things that get covered, and not because anyone's ordered to. It might be softer than that. It might just be what everyone in the building knows the owner likes." She paused. "I don't think those cancel out. I think they're both true and I have to hold them at the same time."

Michelle said, "That's a dialectic, basically. Thesis, antithesis, whatever comes out of the collision."

"That's not exactly what it means," Jessa said.

"It's close enough," Michelle said.

Mr. Khoury, who had been writing nothing on the board this whole time, finally spoke. "So what would you need to know, Juliette, to decide which way that paper leans?"

"That's the thing," she said. "There might not be a fact that settles it. There might just be better and worse questions." She thought of her mother's hands around her coffee cup, the way she'd said, "A paper with an owner is still a paper," and how Juliette hadn't been sure whether that was wisdom or someone inuring herself to what she couldn't change. She didn't say that part out loud. Some things you keep for the essay.

The class argued for twenty minutes about whether a rich owner saving a newspaper was rescue or capture, and Jessa got louder, and Michelle conceded a point for the first time in recorded history, and nobody resolved anything. When the bell rang, Mr. Khoury asked for eight hundred words by Friday, "with evidence, not vibes," and the room emptied the way rooms do, all at once and loudly.

Juliette took down the two front pages last, peeling the tape carefully so she could use them again. At the door she stopped and looked back at the blank whiteboard where they'd hung.

"Rescue and capture," she said to Mr. Khoury. "Same event."

"Maybe," he said, and picked up his markers.

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: Both countries gain from trade only if the exchange rate between the two goods falls between the two countries' own opportunity costs of making them.
story:
The mason jars clinked in the crate as Alex carried them down his grandfather's back steps, past the plum tree his great-grandfather had planted, the whole lineage of the property folded into one crooked orchard. His grandfather had been keeping bees on this half acre since before Alex was born, and this summer, the summer before college, Alex had been handed the smoker and the hive tool and told, simply, learn it. What he had not expected to learn was arithmetic of a stranger kind, the kind that lived in haggling.

Mr. Levy came up the driveway at nine with a basket of apples balanced on one hip, the way he did every other Saturday in September. He kept the orchard two roads over and no bees, and for years the two men had traded honey for apples with the ceremony of much older men, which was to say they argued about it pleasantly for twenty minutes first.

"Four jars," Mr. Levy said, setting the basket on the picnic table. "Same as always, and still robbery."

"Robbery in your favor," Alex's grandfather said. "Six is fair."

Alex, stacking jars, found himself listening differently this year. In the spring he had helped his grandfather work out what the bees actually cost him, and the numbers had stuck: every hour spent on the hives was an hour not spent on the apple trees at the edge of the yard, and by his grandfather's own tally, one basket of apples from those scraggly yard trees cost him the effort of three jars of honey. He'd been surprised how much the yard apples underperformed Mr. Levy's. He'd also, out of curiosity, once asked Mr. Levy how his own bees would do if he ever kept any, and Mr. Levy had laughed and said his wet, shaded land would half drown a hive; a basket of his apples was worth six jars of honey to him, easily.

Alex stood there with his hand on a jar and did the quiet arithmetic twice. Three on one side. Six on the other. Any trade between those two numbers, and his grandfather got apples more cheaply than he could grow them, while Mr. Levy got honey more cheaply than he could ever make it. Below three, his grandfather was better off leaving the apples on his own trees. Above six, Mr. Levy was better off without honey at all. He felt something click that felt less like a math answer and more like a door swinging open onto a room he hadn't known the house contained.

"Six is fair," his grandfather said again, and Alex heard the affectionate theater in it, the ritual of it, and wondered suddenly whether either of them had ever once stated the numbers underneath.

"Three is fair," Mr. Levy said, grinning. "I'll take four and not a jar more."

"Five," said Alex, before he had fully decided to say anything. Both men looked at him. "Between three and six," he went on, a little fast, "you're both winning. Below three, Grandpa, you'd rather grow your own. Above six, Mr. Levy, you'd rather go without. Five's inside it. Four's inside it. You've been arguing for years about a range where neither of you can actually lose."

There was a pause in which Alex worried he had broken something. Then Mr. Levy set the apples down more slowly, the way a man sets down a chess piece he means to think about. "Opportunity cost," he said at last. "That's what the boy's talking about, what you give up to make the thing. My boy's learning that in school." He looked at the honey jars, then at the orchard, then back, as if re-seeing two familiar things laid side by side. "So all this time, the haggling, it was for nothing?"

"It was for the fun of it," Alex's grandfather said, but he said it more quietly than usual, and Alex noticed his thumb moving along the rim of a jar, back and forth. It occurred to Alex that his own argument had a soft spot he couldn't yet close: the rule held only for the two of them, at those two numbers, and the moment prices moved or land changed or one of them got better at something, the whole range would slide. He was honest enough with himself to admit he didn't know where the sliding stopped, or whether somewhere further out there was a trade that looked like this one and quietly drained one side dry. He suspected his economics professor in the fall would have a word for that too, and he suspected he'd enjoy finding it.

They settled on five jars, out of deference to the new arithmetic, and Mr. Levy carried the crate to his truck. Halfway there he turned and looked at the hives glinting past the plum tree, and then at his own apples, one of which he tossed underhand to Alex.

"Next week," Mr. Levy said, "we try four and a half, just to watch your grandfather's face."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: French engineer Maximilien Ringelmann, publishing in 1913, found that people pulling a rope in a group each pulled less hard than they did alone.
story:
The rope ran the length of the gymnasium, looped around the folded-up bleachers, and the whole volleyball team hauled on it in threes while the coach stood at the free-throw line with a stopwatch and a scowl. "That's pathetic," the coach announced. "Clovis pulled that same rope by herself in eleven seconds. Why are six of you slower?" Clovis, who had the good humour of someone recently praised, said, "Because I'm subterranean levels of humble, Coach. I was letting the rope win." Naomi, gripping the rough fibre between Mahelie and a girl whose name she kept forgetting, said nothing. Her palms were burning and she was fairly sure she had been pulling hard, or at least pulling in the direction of the bleachers, which was the point.

They ran the drill again and lost to Clovis's solo time by four seconds. Again, five. The coach made them do it until the janitor's cart squeaked into the far corner as a kind of warning, and then she dismissed them with the particular disgust reserved for teams that lose to arithmetic. In the change room, Mahelie sat on the bench pulling her sock over a blister and expatiated on the injustice of it, at length, in the manner of someone who had once won a debate medal. "The rope doesn't care how many of us there are," she said. "If anything it should move faster. Six sets of arms. Basic addition."

"It's not addition," Naomi said. "It's something else."

"You have a theory?" Clovis threw a towel at her. "You always have a theory."

Naomi did have a theory, or the beginning of one, and it had arrived the way her theories usually did, sideways, during a moment she should have been thinking about something else. Earlier that term, Ms. Chowdhury had set a physics assignment on friction, and Naomi, procrastinating in the library at nine at night, had typed "pulling" and "force" into a search bar and fallen down a hole of old engineering papers. Somewhere between the pages she had found a French engineer, Maximilien Ringelmann, who published in 1913 the results of an experiment with people pulling on a rope. His finding was plain enough that she'd read it three times to be sure she hadn't missed a clause: people pulling in a group each pulled less hard than they did alone.

She remembered sitting in the library carrel with the radiator ticking, feeling the small ugly satisfaction of a suspicion confirmed, and also, immediately, the suspicion's shadow: if it was true of everyone, it was true of her too. There was a flashback quality to the memory even though it was only weeks old, the green library lamp, the highlighter she'd held without uncapping. She had wanted to be an iconoclast about it, to bring the paper to the coach like evidence for the defence. Your Honour, my client was not lazy; my client was experiencing 1913.

At practice the next afternoon she did bring it, printed, folded into quarters in her shoe. She waited until the rope came out again and then, while the coach re-tied the loop, Naomi said, "Can I try something? Everybody pull alone first. One at a time, all the way." The coach looked at her with the flat patience of a woman who had heard many theories, but Mahelie was already volunteering, and one by one they hauled the rope solo while Naomi clocked them. Then six together. Then solo again, quickly, before their arms could argue. The pattern held all afternoon, and it was not subtle. Alone, every one of them pulled harder than she had in the group. Every single one.

"So we're slackers," said the girl whose name Naomi now knew was Priya's replacement, whose actual name she still didn't know. "Great. Solved."

"It's not slackers." Naomi was stacking cones, talking fast. "It's people. It happened in 1913, in France, to an engineer with a rope. Regular people, pulling together, pulled less hard than they did alone. It's not about our character. It's about the group." Mahelie, who had been quiet in a suspicious way, said, "So what do we do about it, since we can't play volleyball one at a time?"

That was the part Naomi had been turning over all through the shuttle run, the part she hadn't solved, the honest hole in the middle of her theory. She stopped stacking. "I don't know yet," she said. "Maybe the knowing helps. Maybe knowing is half of it." She looked at the rope, still looped around the bleachers, and at her team, red-faced and hydrated and lined up like a jury. "Okay. Same drill. But this time, everyone call out one pull. Just your own. Loud."

Mahelie grinned, wrapped her hands, and set her feet. "My rope," she announced to the gymnasium at large. "Nobody else's. Watch me."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: The Hindu festival of Holi falls on the full moon of the month Phalguna, usually in March, and begins with a bonfire the night before called Holika Dahan.
story:
Hudson had been at his grandmother's house for exactly four hours, and in that time he had been asked about his college plans eleven times, which he counted on his fingers behind the mango tree. The twelfth ask came from his aunt while she handed him a plate of gujiya, and he said "undecided" with such brightness that she squinted at him the way one squints at a suspicious receipt.

The real event was tonight. His grandmother's yard had been claimed for a bonfire, wood stacked in a rough pyramid taller than the gate, and by dusk the whole lane smelled of smoke and marigolds. His cousins had explained it to him in fragments, arguing with each other over the fragments. What Hudson gathered was this: tomorrow morning there would be colors, powder thrown, water, anarchy, everyone fair game. Tonight was something else, something older and quieter, a fire lit on the full moon of the month Phalguna, which usually meant March, though his grandmother kept a printed calendar with dates circled in red that clearly outranked the sky.

"It's called Holika Dahan," said Vincenzo, who lived two doors down and had attached himself to the household the way cats attach to whoever feeds them. Vincenzo was not Hindu, but he had opinions about all fires on principle. "The bonfire the night before the colors. My grandmother says it burns away the bad stuff from the whole year."

"Your grandmother is Catholic," Massimo said. He was stretched across the courtyard wall like a cat himself, peeling an orange in one unbroken spiral, which he did whenever he wanted to look unbothered.

"Catholics know about burning things," Vincenzo said, with dignity.

Hudson had texted Ms. Chukwu, his old chemistry teacher, because she was the only adult he knew who answered a question instead of expanding it into a lecture. She had replied with a single line, "Look up the lunar calendar yourself, Hudson," which was less helpful than she probably thought, except that he did, crouched by the router, and found it. The full moon. Phalguna. The fire came first and the colors after, one festival split into two moods. It was, he thought, like a colloquialism he'd once had to explain to a cousin from Delhi, "break a leg," a phrase whose actual words told you nothing and whose meaning everyone somehow agreed on anyway.

The lighting happened without ceremony he could recognize. His grandmother circled the wood with something in her hand, murmuring, and then a match, and the fire took with a low exhale like the whole yard sighing. Sparks went up in a slow column toward the moon, which hung there, full and smug, as if it had personally scheduled itself. The kids were given strict instructions about the noxious smoke, which meant, of course, that they immediately stood downwind of it, coughing and delighted.

"Tomorrow," said a small cousin, pointing at Hudson with a finger already yellow from turmeric, "you will be pink. Completely pink. In your ears."

"I have been informed," Hudson said gravely. "I have made my peace."

Massimo dropped off the wall. "You realize," he said, "this is the only religion festival I've ever seen where the punishment for attending is getting dye in your ears for a week."

"It's not punishment," Hudson began, and then stopped, because he wasn't sure. Vincenzo's grandmother had said the fire burned away the bad of the year, and his own grandmother had said something in a dialect he half-understood about a demoness and a boy who survived, and his aunt had said it was about spring, honestly, mostly spring. Three explanations, none contradicting, none sufficient. He stood with his hands out toward the heat and tried to hold all of them, the way you hold three oranges at once, knowing at any moment one goes rolling.

He thought about saying something to Massimo, something like: maybe it's both, the burning and the pink, the serious night and the ridiculous morning, and maybe you don't have to pick. But Massimo would have teased him for a month, and Hudson wasn't even sure he believed it yet, only that he was testing it, turning it in his hands the way Massimo turned his orange spiral, checking whether it held its shape.

His grandmother appeared beside him, smelling of ghee and smoke, and pressed something into his palm. It was a small packet of pink powder, folded in newspaper, for the morning. "For you," she said. "So they cannot attack you. Only fair."

"A preemptive strike," Hudson said.

"A what?"

"Nothing. Thank you, Dadi."

She patted his cheek and moved off toward the aunt who was already re-filling his plate, and Hudson closed his hand around the packet. His grandmother had armed him with pink. He turned to show Vincenzo, and found Vincenzo already covering him in yellow from a fistful he had, apparently, brought his own supply of, dusting Hudson's hair, his shoulders, his one clean shirt, while Massimo laughed so hard he fell back over the wall, and somewhere behind them all the fire snapped on toward the moon.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: Researcher Amy Edmondson described 'psychological safety' in 1999 as a team's shared belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks, such as admitting a mistake.
story:
Tyler sat at the spartan desk in his bedroom, the robotics logbook open under the desk lamp, and tried to write down what he actually thought about Finley's code for the arm. Three sentences, then two of them crossed out. The problem was not that he had nothing to say. He had too much, and all of it sounded like either a lecture or a lie.

At school that afternoon, Ms. Yip had kept them five minutes past the bell to talk about the competition on Saturday. "You are a team," she had said, which was the kind of thing adults said, and then she had added something stranger: "Ariella, when you found the wiring fault last month, you apologized for four minutes before you told us. I want you to think about why that was necessary." Ariella had gone pink and looked at the floor tiles as if they owed her money.

The team had fallen quiet after that, and Tyler had fallen quiet with them, because he remembered what nobody had said. Two meetings ago, everyone had known the arm's grip sensor was misreading, everyone had watched the test block drop four times in a row, and nobody had mentioned it, because Finley had built the sensor mount and Finley's father had just left, and the silence in the room had a weather to it, something you did not walk out into. The error had metastasized from there, small and ignored, until the whole schedule slipped a week. That was the part that kept Tyler up. The kindness everyone was offering had cost them the same as cruelty would have.

He looked up the thing Ms. Yip had hinted at, half-remembered from a podcast, and found it fast: a researcher named Amy Edmondson, in 1999, describing psychological safety, a team's shared belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks, such as admitting a mistake. He read it twice. He had assumed safety meant something physical, helmets and goggles, or emotional, a general warmth. This was narrower and stranger. It was a belief the team held together, or didn't, about whether you could raise your hand and say the broken thing is mine.

He texted Ariella, mostly to avoid writing. "Are you still mad at Ms. Yip?" Her reply came in pieces. "A little. Mostly mad at myself." Then: "I knew the sensor mount was cracked before the last build. I didn't say it because Finley would know I'd seen his dad's car gone from the lot, and I didn't want him thinking I was watching his life instead of the robot." Tyler put the phone face down on the desk. So it had not been one silence. It had been a small archipelago of them, each person isolated on their own considerate island, and the water between them full of things unsaid.

He tried again in the logbook. Not "the mount is bad," which was true and useless. Not "everything looks great," which was kind and worse than useless. He wrote: "The sensor mount cracked along the print layers. It needs a reprint at forty percent infill, and a support from the left. I should have caught it when it dropped the block the second time and said so then." He read it aloud in the quiet room and heard his own confession sitting there at the end, awkward, necessary.

The next morning Finley was already in the lab, hunched over the printer. Tyler put the logbook on the bench between them, open to the page, and said, "That's what I've got. The specific part and the part that's on me." Finley read it without touching it, the way you read a letter you suspect is bad news. Then he laughed, once, not warmly. "I've known about the crack since Tuesday. I was waiting to see if anyone else would say it." He turned the mount over, and Tyler saw the hairline, and beside it a line of superglue Finley had already laid down. "I glued it at home instead of reprinting because I couldn't face walking in here and saying I broke the one part that was mine."

"Ms. Yip calls the other thing psychological safety," Tyler said. "Whether we believe we can take the risk of admitting a mistake. Edmondson, 1999." Finley frowned at him. "That's the nerdiest thing anyone has ever said to me before nine a.m." But he said it lightly, and he pried the glued mount off the bench and dropped it in the scrap bin himself. "Forty percent infill, support on the left," he repeated, typing. "You're doing the reprint with me. If it fails, we both admit it."

It did not fail cleanly. The new mount printed with a warp on the right side that cost them most of Thursday evening, and Ariella, elbow-deep in the rewiring, said that honestly the old one had dropped the block more gracefully, which made Finley throw a foam dart at her head and miss. Saturday was still going to be close, closer than if someone, anyone, had spoken a week earlier. Tyler filed that away as the price, the part you couldn't refund. On the way out, Ariella caught his sleeve. "If I'd said what I knew when I knew it," she said, and stopped, and he waited, and she only said, "Saturday. Don't glue anything."

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: In West Virginia v. Barnette (1943), the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that public schools cannot force students to salute the flag or recite the Pledge of Allegiance.
story:
The marble stairs of city hall were still cold at nine in the morning, and Kaitlyn climbed them carrying two folders, one for each side of Tinker v. Des Moines, the case she had drawn for the regional mock court exhibition. The assignment was unusual: each competitor had to argue for the petitioner and then, after a ten-minute recess, turn around and argue the opposite. Ms. Kovalenko had called it an exercise in intellectual honesty, though she had refused to say anything more, which Kaitlyn found both irritating and, secretly, a little thrilling.

She found Bianca and Maximus in the council chamber, where folding tables had been arranged into a pretend bench and rows of chairs served as the gallery. Maximus was already gesticulating at the empty bench, practicing an objection he would never get to make, his hands carving shapes in the air as though the judges were already seated. "You look like you're directing traffic," Bianca said, and he dropped his hands, unembarrassed.

"What's it like," Bianca asked Kaitlyn, "having to argue against yourself? Doesn't it feel like lying twice?"

"I don't know yet," Kaitlyn said. She meant it as a dodge, but it came out truer than she intended. She had spent two weeks on the side of the school, building the case that principals could limit student expression to protect order, and she had begun to believe it, the way you begin to believe a character you're writing. The other folder, the students' side, was thinner. That worried her.

A sophomore from another school, waiting for her own round, sat down beside them and asked whether the mock judges could really make the gallery stand for the pledge the way a real courtroom did. "Can they make you stand?" she said. "Like in school?"

Maximus didn't even look up from his notes. "No. West Virginia v. Barnette, 1943. The Supreme Court ruled six to three that public schools cannot force students to salute the flag or recite the Pledge of Allegiance." He said it the way he said everything, fast and flat, like a vending machine dispensing case law.

"Six to three," Kaitlyn repeated. Something rearranged itself quietly in her head. She had known the case existed, had even cited it in a footnote, but she had never thought about the number. Six justices on one side, three on the other, which meant three people whose reasoning she had never read, three people who thought the school should win. She wondered what they had seen that she hadn't. Wasn't that exactly what she needed for her second argument?

During the recess she found the dissenting opinion in Ms. Kovalenko's photocopied packet, sitting in the back row of folding chairs with her finger holding her place. The dissent was careful, circumspect even, the way people are when they know they're losing, and Kaitlyn recognized the feeling of writing that way, hedging every sentence. In biology they had just covered speciation, how one population drifts apart until the two groups can no longer interbreed, and she caught herself thinking that arguments did that too. Her two folders had started as one case and had drifted so far apart that they could not share a sentence anymore. She wasn't sure that was a strength or a failure.

When the round resumed, she argued the school's side first, cleanly, and watched the three volunteer judges, actual law students, one of whom kept tugging her sleeve over her wrist. Then came the recess, and instead of just reordering her notes, Kaitlyn stood at the front of the empty chamber and tried an experiment. She spoke the students' argument in the voice of the Barnette dissent, took the school's own premises and followed them somewhere the school would not want them to go. It felt less like switching sides and more like standing in the middle and letting both arguments pass through her at once. She could not tell whether the position she was assembling was genuinely hers or merely the residue of the two she had performed.

Bianca appeared in the doorway, jacket on, holding out Kaitlyn's water bottle. "They're ready for you."

"Did you know Barnette was six to three?" Kaitlyn asked, gathering the folders, both of which now looked equally worn.

"Three people dissented?"

"Three people dissented."

Bianca shrugged, as if to say that judges were people too, and Kaitlyn walked back toward the bench, wondering which of her two selves would be standing there when she opened her mouth.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: To compare leases fairly, add the rent to every recurring cost the tenant pays, such as heat, electricity, water, internet and insurance, to get a total monthly cost.
story:
The driving school on Route 9 smelled of burnt coffee and vinyl, and every Saturday morning Cole sat in the back row with a folder of apartment printouts while Mr. Berg droned about blind spots. Cole had folded the printouts into quarters so they would fit under his trig notebook, and between videos about merging he unfolded them on his knees: two leases, one for a third-floor walk-up on Marion Street at nine hundred a month, one for a basement unit near the tracks at seven-fifty. Deegan wanted the basement. Deegan had already told everyone at lunch it was basically decided, and Cole had not argued yet, because arguing without numbers felt like just having a taste and calling it a reason.

"Put those away," Mr. Berg said during the break, not unkindly. He was a large man who had been teaching parallel parking for thirty years and treated every personal item in his classroom like a distraction from the single important fact that cars kill people. But then Mara leaned over from the next seat and asked what the papers were, and Mr. Berg, who had a mortgage and a son and opinions about money, pulled a chair around backwards and sat with his arms folded on its back.

Mara read both leases faster than Cole had. "The Marion Street one's more," she said. "Nine hundred against seven-fifty. That's a hundred and fifty a month. That's real."

"Except look," Cole said, and his finger found the line he'd been circling all week. The Marion Street lease said heat and water were included. The basement lease said tenant pays all utilities, and it said it in a small paragraph near the end that Deegan admitted he hadn't read. Cole had asked his mother last night what electricity cost in a basement in winter and she had laughed in a way that was not reassuring. He had texted the basement landlord's agent about average bills and gotten back a single sentence: varies.

Mr. Berg snorted. "Varies means high," he said. "In my day they called that burying the number." He would not say more; he was clear that leases were not his subject and he was not going to hold a seminar, and he got up to reload the coffee machine while Cole and Mara and Deegan spread the two leases across two desks.

That was when Cole did the thing that changed the afternoon. He took out a fresh sheet and drew a line down the middle, and on each side he wrote the rent, and then underneath it he started adding every cost that came every month no matter what: heat, electricity, water, internet, renter's insurance. The agent's "varies" became, after two calls from the hallway, a hundred and ninety for utilities and thirty for insurance. Internet was quoted by both buildings at the same price. When he added it all down, the basement came to over a thousand a month, and Marion Street, with heat and water included, came to nine hundred and eighty-something.

"So the cheap one is the expensive one," Mara said, slow, like she was testing the sentence. "To compare them you have to add the rent to every recurring cost and get the total monthly cost."

"Total monthly cost," Cole repeated, and wrote it at the top of the sheet.

Deegan did not take it well. He excoriated the printouts, the phone calls, the sheet itself, calling the whole exercise a travesty of budgeting because Cole's utility numbers were estimates, not bills, and because "varies" could vary downward, couldn't it. His voice got loud enough that Mr. Berg told them all, from the doorway, that this was a driving school and not a housing court. But when Cole pointed out that even if the basement's utilities came in forty dollars under the estimate, it still wouldn't beat Marion Street, Deegan went quiet, and then he picked up the Marion Street lease and read the included-heat clause twice.

"You changing your mind?" Mara asked him.

"I'm looking," Deegan said, which from Deegan was practically a conversion.

There was a catch, of course, and Mara found it before Cole did. The Marion Street rent of nine hundred was an opening offer; after the first year it went to nine-sixty, and the walk-up was four floors, and the windows faced a wall. The basement, for all its buried numbers, had a door that opened onto grass and a landlord who let you paint. Cole sat with his sheet and understood that the totals made the choice honest without making it easy. He believed the numbers and he did not know yet what they were worth against a patch of grass, and he was tired enough of not knowing that he said so out loud, and Mara said, "That's fair," and Deegan said nothing, still reading.

At the end of class Mr. Berg collected the attendance sheet, paused by their desks, and looked at Cole's column of figures for a long moment. "Good sheet," he said. Then, gathering his keys, he added that his son had once picked an apartment on a parochial little courtyard and spent two years listening to a train, and that no column of numbers had warned him about the train.

Cole laughed, and then stopped, because he was still holding both leases, and the Marion Street unit, the one whose true cost he had just proven lower, was the one near the tracks.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A note one octave higher than another vibrates at exactly twice its frequency, so the A above A440 is 880 hertz.
story:
The community center rented out its back room on Tuesdays to anyone with five dollars and a willingness to be terrible at something in public. Xavier had brought his grandfather's old guitar, a tuner clipped to its headstock, and the private hope that by the end of the month he would no longer sound like a raccoon falling down stairs. Royce had come along to supervise, which meant sitting on a folding chair eating vending machine chips and offering commentary.

"You're flat again," Royce said, without looking up from his phone.

"I'm aware." Xavier plucked the string and watched the little screen on the clip. He'd been chasing an A all evening, and the needle kept sagging left of center. Beside him, Carissa was setting up her own guitar, the one her aunt had left behind when she moved to Tucson. Carissa had claimed she was also a beginner, but Xavier had heard her play in the hallway last week, and beginners did not sound like that.

Ms. Mendoza, who ran the room and tuned pianos for the school district on weekends, drifted past their corner. "Remember," she said, "the tuner's a mirror, not a judge. It just tells you where you are." Then she went to argue with a collapsing music stand, and the stand, in Xavier's opinion, won.

He got the A in tune finally, the needle locking dead center, the number 440 sitting in the corner of the little screen.
